true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `downsize` definition silently overwrites the first in Ruby

Ruby does not support method overloading: defining `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined at line 145. Any existing caller passing separate width and height (5 positional arguments including opts) will now raise ArgumentError, breaking thumbnail/downsize paths that use the old signature. The two signatures must be merged into one method that handles both forms.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores configured per-type size settings

Replacing `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a constant `10 * 1024` breaks the admin-configured contract for both images and attachments: sites that lowered `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` will now accept files client-side that the server/model then rejects (or expensively downsizes), and sites that raised the limit above 10 MB will have valid uploads blocked client-side. The same regression is repeated for the 413 handler at line 246, which also now always reports 10 MB even for attachment uploads.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle as WxH dimensions

`downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which passes `dimensions` to `gifsicle --resize-fit`. The new caller in UploadsController passes `"80%"`, but gifsicle expects a `WIDTHxHEIGHT` geometry, not a percentage, so animated GIFs that exceed the size limit will fail to be downsized (or error out) while the upload loop keeps retrying, and the oversized GIF is ultimately rejected or stored unshrunk.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and proceeds with an oversized upload

The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value and never verifies the result after the loop. If `convert` fails (unsupported format such as SVG, corrupt image, missing tool) or 5 reductions of 20% are not enough, execution falls through to `Upload.create_for` with the still-oversized tempfile, producing an opaque validation failure instead of a meaningful error, after wasting up to 5 external-process invocations.

Hardcoded 10 MB remote-download and unbounded direct-upload downsizing invite resource exhaustion

The API URL branch now always downloads up to 10 megabytes regardless of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`, and the new downsize block runs ImageMagick (up to 5 passes) on any image tempfile above the limit with no upper bound on its incoming size. A user can supply a very large/high-resolution image (within the web server's body limit) and force repeated decompression/conversion of it in the deferred job, consuming disproportionate CPU/memory; previously the download was capped at the configured image limit and oversized files were rejected cheaply by validation.

In-place ImageMagick conversion reads and writes the same file

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert <path>[0] ... <same path>`. ImageMagick is not guaranteed to handle in-place conversion safely: the output file can be truncated/created before the input is fully read, corrupting the upload (especially on failure mid-write, the original tempfile is destroyed). Convert to a separate temp file and atomically replace the original only on success.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes on a nil host instead of returning a validation error

self.host.sub! is called unconditionally in before_validation. Creating an EmbeddableHost with a blank/missing host (reachable from Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#create when the admin submits an empty host) raises NoMethodError on nil instead of failing validates_format_of and rendering a JSON error, producing a 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Update/destroy crash with 500 for a non-existent host id

update and destroy use EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first, which returns nil for a stale or invalid id, then call save_host(nil)/nil.destroy. This raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a 404/not-found response, e.g. when two admins delete/edit the same host concurrently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration inserts un-normalized hosts via unsanitized raw SQL

Legacy embeddable_hosts values such as 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234' are interpolated directly into INSERT without the protocol/path stripping performed by EmbeddableHost.before_validation and without SQL escaping. The stored host therefore will not match EmbeddableHost.record_for_host, which compares lower(host) to the bare URI hostname, so migrated sites silently lose embed access; a value containing a single quote also breaks or injects into the INSERT.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Category and embeddable_host fabricators were swapped into each other's files

category_fabricator.rb now contains only Fabricator(:embeddable_host), while embeddable_host_fabricator.rb contains all the :category/:diff_category/:happy_category/:private_category fabricators. Fabrication loads by scanning files so tests may still pass, but the misplacement makes the fabricators hard to find and risks duplicate-definition or missing-definition errors if either file is later edited, moved, or selectively loaded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration inserts un-normalized hosts via unsanitized raw SQL

Legacy embeddable_hosts values such as 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234' are interpolated directly into INSERT without the protocol/path stripping performed by EmbeddableHost.before_validation and without SQL escaping. The stored host therefore will not match EmbeddableHost.record_for_host, which compares lower(host) to the bare URI hostname, so migrated sites silently lose embed access; a value containing a single quote also breaks or injects into the INSERT.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category or uncategorized setting rows are absent

The migration does execute(...)[0]['id'] and execute(...)[0]['value'] without checking for an empty result. On a fresh install or any site that never saved embed_category/uncategorized_category_id in site_settings, [0] is nil and nil['id'] raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and blocking deployment/upgrades.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
Edit action crashes when a host has no resolvable category

edit() does this.get('host.category.id') without a guard. If the host's category_id points to a deleted category or the category is not present in the client-side category list, host.category is undefined and clicking Edit throws a TypeError, making that host uneditable in the admin UI.

Plural embedded hydration inserts undefined entries and discards the ids

For *_ids fields, _hydrateEmbedded maps each id through _lookupSubType and unconditionally deletes the original obj[k]. When the referenced collection is not present in the payload root (or a category is not loaded), _lookupSubType returns undefined, so the model gets an array containing undefined instead of the objects/ids, and the source ids are lost. The singular branch preserves the id when hydration fails; the plural branch does not.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser record

TopicUser.find_by can return nil (for example a logged-in user who opens or is forwarded an unsubscribe link for a topic they have never visited/interacted with, so no topic_users row exists). Lines 107-113 unconditionally call tu.notification_level and tu.save!, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. Use TopicUser.change (which creates the row) or guard/create the record before updating.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Direct TopicUser save bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

Setting notification_level directly and calling save! bypasses TopicUser.change, which is the codebase path that stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, runs observe_after_save callbacks and publishes the /topic/:id MessageBus notification_level_change. Clients already viewing the topic and derived tracking state can therefore keep showing the old watching/tracking level after an unsubscribe until a reload, and the change is not recorded with a reason/time.

Global unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url for every email that uses it

unsubscribe_link is interpolated by Email::MessageBuilder for any mail built with add_unsubscribe_link: true (body and html_part), using template_args merged from the caller's opts. The new template unconditionally references %{unsubscribe_url}, but only UserNotifications#send_notification_email supplies unsubscribe_url; any other current/future caller with add_unsubscribe_link and no unsubscribe_url will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or render a broken link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be conditional or a default unsubscribe_url should be provided, and no new spec covers the unsubscribe controller action or an email built without unsubscribe_url.

State-changing unsubscribe is exposed as an unauthenticated-token GET request The unsubscribe action mutates notification_level on a plain GET, requires only the ambient login cookie (ensure_logged_in) and skips check_xhr. Any cross-site page can force a logged-in victim's browser to request /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe (e.g. via an tag) and downgrade/mute arbitrary topics for that victim without CSRF protection or a per-user/per-topic signed token. Email unsubscribe links should carry an unguessable token, or require a confirmation POST.

Unsubscribe action is not idempotent and progressively mutes the topic

If notification_level is above regular it is set to regular, otherwise it is set to muted. Re-opening the same email link, refreshing the landing page, or a mail scanner/prefetcher hitting the link a second time therefore takes a user who already unsubscribed (regular) and mutes the topic, which also removes it from topic lists — a stronger effect than requested. Repeated hits should converge on one terminal level (regular), not toggle downwards on each GET.

Unsubscribe template path does not match the topicUnsubscribe route

The Ember route is the top-level route 'topicUnsubscribe' (app-route-map.js.es6 line 13, routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6), whose template name resolves to 'topic-unsubscribe'. The template is instead placed at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which registers as 'topic/unsubscribe' (a nested topic route that does not exist). The unsubscribe page will therefore render with a missing/empty template and the notification dropdown in this file will not be shown.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation mutates BlockedEmail statistics and can count one attempt multiple times

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which saves match_count/last_match_at as a side effect of validation. Validation is not the same as a registration attempt: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save` (which validates again), so a `do_nothing` match is counted twice for one signup, and any other code that merely checks validity (forms, console, related saves) inflates the statistics and performs a DB write during a nominally read-only check. Move the counter update out of the validator or make should_block? pure and record the match explicitly at the point of an actual blocked attempt.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and unnormalized

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up `where(email: email)` with the exact string supplied, and neither BlockedEmail nor the validator normalizes case or surrounding whitespace before lookup/storage. A blocked address such as `bad@spam.com` can therefore be bypassed by registering as `Bad@Spam.com`, and administrators can also create duplicate block entries that differ only by case despite the unique index. Normalize (strip/downcase) the email both when saving BlockedEmail records and when checking should_block?.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
rejectedEmails array is shared mutable state on the controller prototype

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` defines one array on the prototype; `pushObject` in createAccount mutates that shared array rather than an instance-owned copy. Rejected addresses therefore persist across controller instances/recreation and can incorrectly mark an email invalid in a later, unrelated account-creation flow. Initialize rejectedEmails per instance (e.g. in init) instead of sharing the prototype array.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of origin equality

The handler accepts a message whenever discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) !== -1, i.e. whenever the sender's origin is any substring of the configured Discourse URL, rather than requiring e.origin to equal the Discourse origin. Origins that are prefixes/substrings of the configured URL are accepted, weakening the check that the resize message actually came from the Discourse embed iframe; the origin should be parsed once and compared exactly.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Full referer URL used as postMessage targetOrigin never matches

postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin (scheme://host:port), but this passes the entire request.referer including its path and query. Browsers compare it against the parent window's origin, so the discourse-resize message is silently never delivered and the embed iframe added by embed.js never gets resized to its content height.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content

i.content is nil for RSS/Atom items that only provide a summary/description (SimpleRSS does not guarantee content), so i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError and aborts the whole hourly poll, preventing all remaining items from being imported. String#scrub also does not exist on the Ruby 1.9/2.0 runtimes this codebase targets, so this raises NoMethodError even when content is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript

request.referer is inserted verbatim inside a single-quoted JS string passed to postMessage. The controller only checks the referer's host, so a referer such as http://<embeddable_host>/'-alert(1)-' contains a quote that breaks out of the string and executes arbitrary script in the embed page on the Discourse origin. The referer must be JS/HTML-escaped (and reduced to an origin) before interpolation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import stores attacker-controlled RSS/Atom or scraped page contents as a Post with cook_method raw_html. Post#cook returns raw verbatim for that method, and the cooked HTML is rendered raw in topic and embed views. No sanitization is applied on this path (PollFeed passes feed content straight through), so a feed item or embedded page containing <script>/event-handler markup becomes stored XSS for every forum visitor who views the imported topic.

Spec expects synchronous TopicRetriever use that the controller no longer performs

This test expects TopicRetriever.new/retrieve to be called during EmbedController#best, but the controller instead calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). The mock expectations can never be satisfied by the implementation under test, so this example fails and provides no coverage of the actual enqueued job arguments (user_id and embed_url).

Unauthenticated requests can flood the retrieve_topic job queue

Every GET for an unknown embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job. The 60-second throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieve, which only runs when a job is executed, not before enqueueing. Anyone who can present the embeddable referer can therefore issue many requests for distinct or identical URLs faster than jobs drain and fill Sidekiq with jobs that each may fetch remote pages/feed content, instead of throttling/deduplicating at enqueue time.

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with no validation

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url) on the supplied URL before TopicEmbed.import's scheme check runs, and performs no host allowlist, private-address, or redirect validation. Callers that pass externally influenced URLs (e.g. thread links from a Disqus export) can make the server issue requests to internal/metadata addresses (SSRF) and import the response. Host validation in TopicRetriever does not protect this entry point.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items() emits invalid/non-standard legacy values and properties

align-items() passes $alignment verbatim to -webkit-box-align, whose 2009-syntax value set is start/end/center/baseline/stretch (not flex-start/flex-end), omits -moz-box-align entirely despite flexbox() emitting -moz-box, and emits -ms-align-items (line 121), which is not a real property (IE10 uses -ms-flex-align, line 120). Current call sites only pass center/baseline so they happen to survive, but as a shared foundation mixin any future align-items(flex-start/flex-end) call will silently do nothing in legacy WebKit and Firefox, producing inconsistent alignment across browsers.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin is off by one for the 2009 flexbox syntax

The order() mixin copies $val verbatim into -webkit-box-ordinal-group/-moz-box-ordinal-group, but the 2009 syntax is 1-based (default ordinal-group is 1 and values < 1 are invalid) while flex order is 0-based (default 0). To emulate order:N on old WebKit/Firefox the ordinal-group must be N+1. As written, order(0) would be invalid/dropped and ordered items are shifted one group toward unordered items, so the legacy-prefixed rendering this mixin exists for (used by .panel order(3) in header.scss and .extra-info-wrapper order(2) in topic.scss) can order header children differently from the standard `order` rendering.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex .small-action loses the right-aligned action button

Making .small-action a flex container (lines 264-265) makes float have no effect on its flex items, including the direct-child button styled `float: right` at lines 306-310. No replacement positioning is added (no margin-left: auto on the button, no justify-content, and .small-action-desc has no flex-grow), so the button that was previously pinned to the right edge of the row now sits immediately after the description text, changing the layout of small-action rows (e.g. topic timer / close / split notices).

Header panel loses all positioning in browsers without flexbox

.panel's `float: right` was replaced with `margin-left: auto` plus `@include order(3)` (lines 35-40), and .title's float was removed in favour of .contents being display:flex (lines 14-19). In browsers with no flexbox support at all (e.g. IE9, which the -webkit-box/-moz-box fallbacks in mixins.scss show this codebase still targets with legacy syntax), margin-left:auto/order are inert and nothing floats or positions the panel, so the header icons/login buttons collapse to the left after the title instead of sitting at the right edge. A float fallback (kept alongside the flex rules, since floats are ignored on flex items) is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing ? so it is never used

ActiveModelSerializers in this codebase gates attributes with methods named `include_<attr>?`, as seen in include_email?, include_card_image_badge_id?, include_stats? and the methods generated by untrusted_attributes. The new method is defined as `include_website_name` without `?`, so the serializer will never call it. Consequently website_name is serialized even when website is blank (as a nil value), and the intended present? check provides no protection; the method must be renamed to `include_website_name?`.

false_positives.candidate:
Displayed website_name drops query string and fragment, so 'complete URL' text can be incomplete/misleading

When the website host matches the instance host, the code returns `website_host + URI(website).path` only. For a website such as http://example.com/?page=user or http://example.com/profile#section the display text becomes just `example.com/` / `example.com/profile`, omitting the query/fragment that distinguish the actual target while the link still points to the full URL. The visible label therefore does not show the complete URL as the PR title promises; query (and fragment) should be appended when present.

website_name is not hidden for untrusted TL0 users viewed anonymously

`website` is listed in untrusted_attributes so it is suppressed when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object) applies (TL0 user seen by anonymous, to prevent spam/abuse harvesting), but the newly added `website_name` attribute at line 43 is not added to that list (lines 105-111) and has no equivalent restriction check. Anonymous visitors therefore still receive the website host and, for same-domain sites, the full path derived directly from the hidden website field, defeating the existing restriction. website_name should be added to untrusted_attributes (or otherwise gated the same way), and the spec's untrusted_attributes list should cover it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Every fallback lookup performs a SiteSetting lookup

FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale on each invocation, and the fallbacks backend invokes [] for translation lookups (including repeated/missing keys). This adds a settings/cache lookup to hot I18n paths that the translate accelerator is specifically trying to keep fast, instead of computing and memoizing the chain per locale and invalidating it when the site locale changes.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, and missed fallbacks get cached

Fallback translations are loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale calling I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Background jobs, mailers, console/rake code and other non-controller paths set I18n.locale without this call, and I18n.translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only loads config.locale. In those contexts a key missing from the primary locale will be looked up in fallback locales whose YAML was never loaded, return a missing-translation string, and for argument-less translations that result is frozen into the LRU cache keyed only by key+locale+backend, poisoning later web requests until reload.

Fallback lookup crashes when SiteSetting/default locale is unavailable

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every fallback computation. Before the database/settings are ready (boot, rake tasks, migrations, asset precompilation, or a nil/blank default_locale) SiteSetting can raise or return nil, and nil.to_sym raises NoMethodError. Because the I18n fallbacks backend invokes this on translation lookups, a routine translation can crash boot or request handling instead of falling back to :en.

I18n.fallbacks is replaced with a Hash that does not implement the Fallbacks API

I18n.fallbacks is assigned a plain Hash subclass whose [] always computes a new array and ignores stored entries. Code and gems expecting the I18n::Backend::Fallbacks object installed by Rails/i18n (e.g. assigning fallbacks per-locale with []=, reading defaults, or calling methods other than the newly added ensure_loaded!) will silently lose assignments or fail. In environments where Rails still sets config.i18n.fallbacks, Rails can also overwrite this object with a real Fallbacks instance that has no ensure_loaded!, making ApplicationController#set_locale raise NoMethodError.

Translation cache ignores the dynamic fallback chain

The LRU cache key is "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}" but the resolved value now depends on FallbackLocaleList, i.e. on SiteSetting.default_locale at lookup time. If an admin changes the site default locale, or a translation is first resolved before its fallback locale is loaded, the cached value for the user locale remains stale/frozen and is served indefinitely (up to cache eviction/reload) instead of the translation from the new fallback locale.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets are passed directly into queryset slicing

When enable_advanced_features is set, a user-supplied cursor offset < 0 is used verbatim as queryset[start_offset:stop]. Cursor strings are attacker-controlled (Cursor.from_string accepts any integer), so an authorized admin/superuser can craft offsets such as -1000000. Django querysets explicitly reject negative indexing with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), causing unhandled 500s, and if this pattern is reused with list-backed querysets it wraps around and returns rows outside the intended page bounds. Other paginators in this file validate this case and raise BadPaginationError; this path adds no validation, bound, or max_offset check.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. For a non-superuser whose organization_context.member is None (e.g. access granted without a member row), this raises AttributeError and breaks the previously working default DateTimePaginator path for all audit-log requests, not just optimized ones. Any optimized request that returns rows (or builds next/prev cursors via build_cursor) will 500 instead of paginating.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change exposes all existing paginated endpoints to negative-offset crashes

The shared BasePaginator.get_result now branches on is_prev: for prev cursors the raw cursor.offset is still passed to queryset[offset:stop], and the comment claims 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. It does not: Django raises AssertionError on negative slices. Because this edits the base class used by every DateTimePaginator/Paginator endpoint, any user who can supply a crafted prev cursor with a negative offset to any existing endpoint can trigger an unhandled 500. The change also silently changes non-prev behavior (clamping to 0) without tests for either direction.

Cursor offset remains unvalidated while PR relies on negative offsets being safe

Cursor.__init__ stores int(offset) with no lower bound, and from_string therefore accepts arbitrary negative offsets from the query string. The added comment asserts this 'enables efficient reverse pagination', but no consumer validates it: SequencePaginator asserts offset > -1, OffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator raise BadPaginationError for negative offsets, and Django querysets raise AssertionError. Landing the comment/behavior contract without central validation leaves each paginator to fail inconsistently (assert, 500, or wrap-around) on the same crafted cursor.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, changes BasePaginator slicing, and adds an optimized branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, but includes no tests. There is no coverage that optimized pagination returns correct next/prev cursors for datetime keys, that negative offsets are rejected rather than crashing or leaking out-of-page rows, or that non-admin/non-optimized requests still work. OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime ordering it is wired into

`get_item_key` does `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute, copying `Paginator` instead of `DateTimePaginator`. `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError` on the first result whenever `optimized_pagination=true` is used by a superuser/global-access member. false_positives.candidate:
Flush-side max_segment_spans guard removed with no replacement for pre-existing/oversized keys

The check that skipped and logged segments with more than `max_segment_spans` spans was deleted from `_load_segment_data`. The only remaining cap is the new Lua insert-time cap of 1000, which does not apply to keys created before this change, keys written by still-running old consumers during a rolling deploy, or the `max_segment_bytes`-only path; such segments are now loaded and flushed regardless of span count, and `self.max_segment_spans` is left as dead configuration.

Insert-time eviction silently discards spans and can produce incomplete segments

When a segment exceeds 1000 members, `zpopmin` silently removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans without any metric, log, or marker that the segment was truncated. The remaining segment is later flushed as if complete. This replaces the previous `_load_segment_data` behaviour of detecting oversized segments and logging/metric-ing `segment_span_count_exceeded`, and changes the cap from `max_segment_spans=1001` in Python to a hardcoded 1000 in Lua, so legitimate large segments lose spans invisibly.

No test exercises eviction, the 1000-span cap, or deep redirect chains

The test changes only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing Span constructions (all with the identical timestamp 1700000000.0). Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify which spans `zpopmin` evicts (including whether the root/segment span can be evicted, invalidating `has_root_span` flushing), nothing verifies ordering by differing `end_timestamp_precise` scores after `zunionstore` merges, and nothing covers redirect chains over 1000 hops. The core new behaviour of the PR is therefore untested, as is the new OptimizedCursorPaginator/audit-log path.

Redirect chain traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop that follows `span-buf:sr:` redirects now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper segment trees may not be joined correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 will now be split into multiple segments (wrong `set_key`, wrong segment/root attribution) where they previously assembled correctly, with no test covering deep chains near the new limit.

Required end_timestamp_precise lookup can crash the consumer on spans lacking the field

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message without that field (the existing consumer test payload did not include it until this PR added it). A single such message fails `process_batch` and, being redelivered, can poison-pill the batch instead of being handled or defaulted. The new `Span.end_timestamp_precise` field in buffer.py is likewise a required positional field, breaking any other `Span(...)` constructors that were not updated.

SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks on existing Redis data during deployment

`process_spans` now `zadd`s to `span-buf:s:*` keys and the Lua script uses `zcard`/`zunionstore`, while `_load_segment_data` uses `zscan`. Any segment keys already stored as plain SETs by the previous version (written with `sadd`) will raise Redis WRONGTYPE errors when touched by the new code, so in-flight segments at deploy time will error out / be lost instead of being flushed. No migration, dual-read, or versioned key prefix is provided.

Unrelated, undocumented optimized_pagination switch changes audit-log API behaviour

This PR is described as a spans-buffer optimization, but it adds a new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter and a superuser/`has_global_access` gate that swaps the audit-log endpoint to a different paginator class. That is an unreviewed API contract/behaviour change bundled into the spans change: cursor format and results now depend on the caller's privileges, and (per the paginator defects) the privileged path is broken, with no endpoint tests covering either branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key relies on Python hash() and the invalidation helper is never wired up

Eligibility is cached under a key built from hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) and invalidate_upsampling_cache recomputes the same expression, but no code path calls invalidate_upsampling_cache when the project allowlist option changes. Combined with hash-collision risk between different project sets, one project set can briefly serve another set's cached eligibility and, more importantly, allowlist removals keep upsampling (and additions keep not upsampling) until TTL expiry with no invalidation hook despite the helper suggesting otherwise. Use a deterministic, collision-resistant key (e.g. the joined project ids) and either call invalidation on option change or remove the dead helper.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset (which the dashboard-widget split logic can change to discover or keep as the metrics dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead of scoped_dataset. When a metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced request is split into a Discover error query, upsampling is wrongly skipped; conversely a transaction-like split can be transformed based on the original dataset even though the executed dataset/query is not error data. The transform decision must be made for the dataset actually executed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental gitlink/subproject file committed

This adds a file `sentry-repo` containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a', i.e. an accidental nested-repository gitlink. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, will confuse tooling/checkouts, and should be removed before merge.

Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query inspects request.GET['query'], but _get_event_stats executes the `query` argument passed through get_event_stats_data and the dashboard split logic, which can differ from the raw GET parameter (split code appends 'AND !event.type:transaction', callers can supply modified queries). Eligibility can therefore be decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, causing missed upsampling for split error queries or transforms applied to non-error executions. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility check instead of re-reading the request.

Substring check treats negated error filters as error-focused queries

_is_error_focused_query does a raw substring search for 'event.type:error', so queries such as '!event.type:error', '-event.type:error', or 'event.type:transaction OR !event.type:error' are classified as error-focused. The endpoint will then rewrite count() to sum(sample_weight) over predominantly transaction/non-error rows, where sample_weight is not meaningful/populated, returning zero or badly undercounted series instead of the real count.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no fallback for rows whose sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects will normally contain historical events and events ingested without client sampling information; ClickHouse sum() ignores NULLs (and yields NULL/0 for an all-NULL bucket), so those events silently disappear from upsampled counts rather than counting as 1 each. A safe aggregate needs a per-row default such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

upsampled_count is only registered on Discover but is generated for the errors dataset

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count() whenever _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True, and that helper returns True unconditionally for the errors dataset. However the new SnQLFunction is only added to the Discover dataset's function_converter; the errors dataset has its own function converter without upsampled_count. Any events-stats request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore fail query validation/building (unknown function) instead of returning upsampled counts.

The unit test masks this by using second-scale segment timestamps (1.5/2.0/3.0).

Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching

Single-use backup codes can be replayed concurrently

Consumption is a non-atomic read-check-update: two simultaneous logins with the same backup code can both read the stored array, both find the code at the same index, and both authenticate before either request writes back the array with that entry nulled. The documented 'exactly once' property of backup codes is therefore not enforced under concurrent requests; the code should be consumed with an atomic/conditional update or lock.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code can bypass password verification with a dummy TOTP field

Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, without exempting the new backup-code path. An attacker calling the credentials endpoint directly with a valid backup code, any non-empty totpCode value, and no/wrong password therefore skips verifyPassword, then enters the backupCode branch (which never validates the dummy totpCode) and is authenticated. A backup code, intended only as a second factor, becomes a single-factor passwordless login credential.

Backup codes are persisted and returned before TOTP setup is verified

Setup writes the encrypted backup codes (and TOTP secret) to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the setup response before the user has proven possession of the authenticator by completing the enable step. If setup is abandoned, valid backup codes for a not-yet-enabled account remain stored in the database, and the codes are already exposed to any client/script that called setup, even though the UI only displays them after enabling. Codes should be generated/confirmed at enable time, or at minimum not persisted until enable succeeds.

No test exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The new e2e coverage only downloads/copies the codes during setup; the file itself notes 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. The security-critical behaviors added in this PR — login with a backup code, rejection of a wrong code, single-use invalidation on reuse, missing-codes handling for pre-existing 2FA users, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — have no automated verification, so regressions or bypasses in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts would ship undetected.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.

Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty or null for Google Meet events

The code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. It should use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google updateEvent loses destination-calendar fallback

When externalCalendarId is falsy, `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` compares externalIds against undefined/null and therefore never matches, so selectedCalendar becomes undefined. Previously it fell back to the destination calendar's externalId. calendar.events.update is then called with calendarId undefined, so updates for bookings without an externalCalendarId on the reference fail instead of updating the destination calendar. The fallback should be the first/matching destination calendar, not a find against the falsy argument.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

For a collective event with multiple hosts, the second host's credential is used to create an event on the first host's calendar ID, causing 404/authorization failures or a duplicate event on the wrong calendar rather than an event on the second host's calendar. The per-credential destination must be selected by credentialId.

false_positives.candidate:
Google deleteEvent loses destination-calendar fallback and may delete from primary

When externalCalendarId is falsy, the find compares each destination calendar's externalId to that falsy value and returns undefined, so deleteEvent falls back to `primary`. Previously it used the stored destination calendar. Cancelling a booking whose event lives on a non-primary destination calendar will therefore target the wrong calendar (or 404/be silently resolved) and leave the actual event undeleted.

Lark createEvent always uses first host's destination calendar for every host

EventManager loops over all destination calendars and creates one event per credential, but Lark's createEvent still derives calendarId solely from `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. A collective booking's additional hosts therefore attempt creation on the organizer's Lark calendar with their own credentials, which fails or writes to the wrong calendar, so the multi-host fix does not work for Lark. It needs to pick the destination whose credentialId matches the credential used for this call.

Non-credential destinations create events without storing externalCalendarId/credentialId correctly

In the branch where a destination has no credentialId, createAllCalendarEvents calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing destination.externalId (unlike the credentialId branch at line 370). EventResult.externalId is therefore undefined, and referencesToCreate stores externalCalendarId undefined for that calendar event. Subsequent reschedule/cancel/update operations cannot address the specific external calendar the event was created on and may target primary/the wrong calendar.

Recurring cancellation deletes the first calendar reference for every credential and repeats per outer reference

Inside the new loop over all bookingCalendarReference entries, the recurring branch maps over all organizer calendar credentials and for each updated booking uses `updBooking.references.find(ref => ref.type.includes('_calendar'))`, i.e. always the first calendar reference regardless of the credential being iterated or the outer reference. With multiple hosts/references this issues duplicate deleteEvent calls with mismatched credential/uid/externalCalendarId pairs, potentially failing to delete some hosts' events and repeatedly deleting others.

Team destination calendars are silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null

evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizerUser has a destination calendar, and team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. With null, the optional-chain push is a no-op, so for a collective event where only non-organizer hosts have destination calendars, those calendars are lost and EventManager falls back to creating only one event on the first generic calendar credential. Initializing to [] or assigning the team array would preserve them.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricates dummy refresh_token and strips real token fields when sharing is enabled

Server schema allows duplicate, case-variant, and unbounded guest lists

An API caller can therefore create duplicate attendee rows (e.g. 'A@x.com' and 'a@x.com', or the same email twice, causing createMany duplicates) and submit arbitrarily large lists to spam calendar invites/emails. Team admin/owner check requires being both admin and owner

A team admin who is not the owner (and vice versa) therefore evaluates to false, so legitimate team admins/owners who are not also the booking organizer or an attendee get FORBIDDEN. Any attendee can add arbitrary guests to someone else's booking

Authorization passes if the caller is merely an attendee (matched by email). The UI only exposes this action on the organizer's bookings page, but via the API any attendee with a Cal.com account can add unlimited arbitrary guests to the organizer's booking, triggering calendar updates and invitation emails from the organizer without organizer approval. This is a privilege escalation beyond the organizer-only feature being added.

Calendar is updated with the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

credentials are loaded via getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and EventManager is built from the calling user, while evt.destinationCalendar belongs to the booking organizer. When the caller is a team admin or attendee (both explicitly authorized above), the organizer's calendar event is updated using the wrong user's credentials, so the calendar update will fail or target the wrong account even though the DB attendees were already added. Credentials/EventManager should be based on booking.user (already loaded with credentials in the query).

No booking status or timing check before adding guests

The handler never checks booking.status or start/end time. Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, pending, or already-ended bookings; the handler then persists attendees, calls updateCalendarAttendees, and sendAddGuestsEmails emits ICS files with status CONFIRMED. This can resurrect/confuse dead bookings and sends misleading confirmed invites for events that will not happen. It should reject non-accepted and past bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increment uses stale snapshot instead of atomic increment

Both increments write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read by the earlier findMany. If two cron invocations (or overlapping executions of the same invocation window) process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both read the same count and both write the same count+1, losing an increment; likewise a concurrent successful scheduling can be overwritten in effect because the failure writer does not condition on scheduled:false. This lets a permanently failing reminder be attempted more than the intended two times and makes the >1 deletion threshold unreliable. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` (ideally guarded by scheduled:false).

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

Retry-count deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The deleteMany OR's second branch only checks retryCount > 1, without method: WorkflowMethods.SMS (and without scheduled: false). Because WorkflowReminder rows are shared by EMAIL, SMS and WHATSAPP methods, any non-SMS reminder whose retryCount ever exceeds 1 will be deleted by this SMS cron, losing its referenceId/cancellation handle even though this job never processed it. The SMS-only condition from the original first branch does not carry over to the second OR branch.

Missing recipient or empty message never increments retryCount

If sendTo is null/empty (e.g. booking has no smsReminderNumber / step has no sendTo) or the rendered message is empty, neither branch runs: the reminder stays scheduled:false with retryCount 0 and is re-fetched and re-processed on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes. This is one of the permanent-failure modes the PR is meant to bound, so those reminders are still retried indefinitely.

Unhandled update in catch block can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits prisma.workflowReminder.update without any nested error handling. If that update rejects (e.g. the reminder was deleted by the top-of-run deleteMany of a concurrent invocation, a booking-cancellation cleanup, or a transient DB error - Prisma throws P2025 for a missing record), the exception propagates out of the per-reminder loop, the handler returns 500, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are never processed in this run. Previously the catch only logged and the loop continued.

Authorization fragments return unparenthesized top-level OR conditions

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition (and the team equivalent at line 196-207) returns SQL of the form `(team condition) OR (user condition)` with no outer parentheses, and getFilterConditions likewise returns an unparenthesized `(eventTypeId = ...) OR (eventParentId = ...)` for a single filter. The org and team authorization tests only assert structural equality of Prisma.sql objects (strings/values); the sole test that executes SQL (line 481) uses user scope, whose condition contains no ANY(array) parameter and no OR branch. Whether Prisma/Postgres binds a JavaScript number[] supplied as `= ANY(${teamIds})` / `= ANY(${userIds})` correctly is therefore unverified, even though org/team insights depend entirely on that binding. Cache status ignores cache expiry

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows for the credentials with no expiresAt filter, while getCachedAvailability only serves rows with expiresAt >= now. Credentials whose cache expired (one month after write) will therefore still report a cacheUpdatedAt in connectedCalendars, display 'Cache Status' in the UI, and offer to delete data that is never actually served.

Deleting cache does not invalidate the connected-calendars query

The deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls onSuccess, unlike disconnectMutation below it which invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations on settle. When onChanged/onSuccess is undefined (or does not refetch), the parent keeps the old query data, so cacheUpdatedAt remains set, the 'Cache Status / Delete cached data' entry stays visible, and the user sees stale status immediately after a successful deletion.

Handler bypasses the calendar-cache disabled/mock repository path

The handler directly instantiates the concrete CalendarCacheRepository instead of going through the CalendarCache initialization that substitutes CalendarCacheRepositoryMock when calendar cache is disabled. Every connectedCalendars request now performs a CalendarCache groupBy query and can surface cache status even for users/organizations where the calendar-cache feature is disabled, adding an unconditional DB query to a hot settings endpoint.

New destructive deleteCache mutation has no tests

This PR adds a mutation that deletes all CalendarCache rows for a credential, guarded only by the credential-ownership check in this new handler, plus the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds repository method, with no tests covering: deleting one's own cache, rejecting another user's credentialId, and returning cache status per credential. A regression in the ownership where-clause would let one user purge another user's calendar cache without any test failing.

On a fresh/offline install npx will try to download an unpinned package from the registry, making the script non-reproducible and failing without network access; tsx should be added as a pinned devDependency or the ts-node invocation kept.

updateManyByCredentialId accepts the wrong Prisma input type

The method types data as Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput but passes it to prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany, which expects SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput. UpdateInput permits nested relation operations (e.g. user: { connect }) that updateMany cannot execute, so the public repository signature promises operations that will fail or fail type-checking at the Prisma call; it should use the UpdateMany mutation input type.

Workflow reminder cancellations are fired without being awaited

updatedBookings.forEach calls the async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder without awaiting or collecting the promises (the same pattern is used in handleNewBooking's reschedule block, where the surrounding try/catch cannot catch async rejections either). The handler can return 'Booking successfully cancelled' before the cancelled=true update (or SMS cancellation/row deletion) has actually been persisted; if the serverless invocation is torn down after the response, the flag is never written and the scheduled reminder email is still sent for the cancelled booking. The cancellation promises should be collected and awaited (e.g. Promise.all over flatMap).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves the WorkflowReminder row neither deleted nor marked cancelled

When immediateDelete is true and a referenceId exists, the function cancels the send at SendGrid and returns without deleting the workflowReminder row or setting cancelled=true. Callers that do not subsequently cascade-delete the row (notably handleNewBooking's reschedule path, where the old booking and its reminders persist) leave a row with scheduled=true pointing at an already-cancelled batch. The stale row is only cleaned up by the cron's past-scheduledDate sweep, and any logic that later iterates the old booking's workflowReminders will try to cancel the same batch again.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
One failed SendGrid cancellation blocks all remaining cancellations in the cron run

The loop over remindersToCancel awaits client.request inside a single try/catch that wraps the whole loop, and the Prisma deletes are only executed after the loop finishes. If cancelling any one reminder fails (e.g. SendGrid error or a stale/null referenceId), the catch aborts the loop: every later reminder is never attempted, and even reminders already cancelled at SendGrid are not deleted from the DB in this run. Worse, the failing reminder stays first in the result set on subsequent runs, so it can poison every 15-minute cron invocation and workflow emails for cancelled/rescheduled bookings keep being sent. Each reminder's cancellation and deletion should be isolated in its own try/catch.

Rescheduled bookings still use immediate SendGrid cancellation, defeating the deferred-cancellation fix

For a reschedule, deleteScheduledEmailReminder is called with immediateDelete=true, which immediately POSTs status=cancel to SendGrid. Per the PR description, cancelled scheduled sends accumulate in SendGrid's scheduled_sends (capped at 100 pending cancellations) until their scheduled date, and once that cap is hit further cancellations fail and the old email is still sent. Reschedules therefore remain subject to exactly the bug this PR claims to fix for rescheduled bookings; they should be marked cancelled=true and left for the scheduleEmailReminders cron to cancel within the last hour, like the cancellation paths do.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach makes calendar/video cancellation fire-and-forget and bypasses try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` is never awaited: forEach ignores the returned promises, and the surrounding try/catch cannot catch rejections from the async callback. Reschedule() proceeds to send the reschedule email and return true before (and regardless of whether) the old calendar/video events are deleted, so failures are silently lost as unhandled rejections and stale events can remain. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are eagerly started, not lazy

Every value is an already-executed import() call in the object literal, so importing appStore immediately initiates loading all ~30 app modules instead of loading only the requested app on first use. This defeats the stated purpose of the PR and keeps the startup/bundle-evaluation cost (and side effects) of every app for any caller that needs just one. The promises should be wrapped in thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with callers invoking them. A related consequence is that a failing optional app creates a rejected promise at import time that may surface as an unhandled rejection even if that app is never used.

requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` discards the promises returned by the async callback. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are never killed before being replaced

Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess objects are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the fork-context Process class). The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard therefore evaluates to False for every real flusher process. When _ensure_processes_alive detects a hang (is_alive() is True but healthy_since is stale), it skips process.kill() and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards. The hung process keeps running alongside its replacement, so two processes can concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produce for the same Redis shards, risking duplicate or racing segment flushes, while the hung process continues consuming resources. The guard should check against the spawn context's process type / BaseProcess, or duck-type on kill/terminate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiprocess flusher test never exercises flushing or restart with multiple processes

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts len(processes)/num_processes and that the shard map totals 4, then immediately joins without submitting any span or advancing drift, so it cannot catch regressions in per-process flushing, duplicate production when shards share a process, backpressure aggregation, or the process-restart path in _ensure_processes_alive. Given the PR's core change is parallel flushing and supervision, a test should push spans through a multi-process (at least multi-thread via produce_to_pipe) flusher and assert each segment is produced exactly once, and/or simulate a dead/hung process and assert it is replaced.

Negative or zero flusher-process configuration crashes or disables flushing

The CLI option --flusher-processes accepts any int with no validation. A negative value flows through factory.py into SpanFlusher, where max_processes stays negative (only 0/None fall back via `or`), num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and the shard assignment loop then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failures when computing i % num_processes or indexing the map. If assigned_shards is empty, num_processes is 0 and no flusher process is ever created while submit() still forwards messages to the committer, so spans can be committed to Redis but never flushed. Validate flusher_processes >= 1 at the CLI/factory boundary and handle the no-shards case explicitly.

join() never terminates spawned flusher processes

join() uses the same isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check before calling process.terminate(). Because the flushers are SpawnProcess objects from the spawn context, this check is always False in production, so any flusher that does not exit promptly after stopped is set is never terminated. join() waits until the deadline for each process in sequence and then silently returns with daemon processes still alive, leaking processes and potentially leaving flushers running against Redis/Kafka after the consumer strategy has shut down. Use the mp_context process base type or hasattr-based termination instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Catch-all in submit marks offsets complete for messages never enqueued

submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except and, on any exception, adds and immediately completes the offset. This conflates poison messages with transient failures: e.g. grouping_fn raising, queue shutdown raising queue.ShutDown, or the real decode_payload asserting on FilteredPayload (decode_payload asserts payload is not FilteredPayload) all cause the offset to become committable even though nothing was processed, silently dropping the message with only a log line.

Committable-offset scan is O(offset range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) and is invoked every second by the commit loop. When one slow item blocks a partition (the exact scenario this PR targets), the outstanding window grows with throughput, so each scan walks an ever-larger range of integers doing two set lookups per offset, and all_offsets keeps every uncommitted offset in memory. A single stuck subscription can thus make commit processing progressively more expensive and delay commits for all partitions.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore advance past a message that was never successfully processed, contradicting the strategy's documented 'only commits after successful processing' guarantee and causing permanent data loss on transient processing failures instead of redelivery.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(group_key) % num_queues. For str keys hash() is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the 'consistent hashing' claimed in the docstring is not stable across restarts or across consumer processes: the same subscription is assigned to a different queue whenever the process restarts, breaking the ordering/affinity guarantee the pool exists to provide relative to any other process or previous incarnation. A stable digest (e.g. md5/sha like other Sentry grouping code) is required.

Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread

_commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls commit_function (the Arroyo Commit callable supplied to create_with_partitions) from there. Arroyo processing strategies are driven single-threaded by StreamProcessor and the commit callable/consumer commit path is not documented as thread-safe; invoking it concurrently with the main consumer loop risks races with the processor's own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit logic and with partition assignment changes, potentially committing offsets for partitions no longer owned.

Queue pool and offset tracker are never reset on partition reassignment

The FixedQueuePool (and its OffsetTracker) is created once in the factory __init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. OffsetTracker state (all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed) is keyed only by Partition and is never cleared when partitions are revoked or reassigned, and last_committed starts at -1 regardless of the committed position Arroyo passes in the partitions mapping. After a rebalance, stale outstanding entries from the previous assignment can permanently block commits for a reassigned partition, or stale last_committed state can cause incorrect committable calculations for a partition this consumer no longer owns or newly owns at a different position.

Strategy close/terminate discards queued work by shutting down the shared pool

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit shutdown event and immediately calls queue_pool.shutdown() without first waiting for queues to drain (wait_until_empty is never used). FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True, so a worker exits at the top of its loop after its current item even if its queue still holds items. On Arroyo partition revocation/rebalance this abandons in-flight messages, and because the same pool is shared (see result_consumer factory), closing one strategy instance also kills the pool for any subsequently created strategy: queue.put then raises queue.ShutDown, which submit()'s catch-all converts into add+complete offset, silently committing unprocessed messages.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can grow without limit

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns immediately after put(). Despite the docstring claiming natural backpressure, the Arroyo consumer will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing messages as fast as it can fetch them even if workers are stuck or slow, leading to unbounded in-memory growth/OOM and a huge backlog of fetched-but-uncommitted offsets.

false_positives.candidate:
Shard-split queries are interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery() already maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) because it needs the interpolated selector to fetch __stream_shard__ values, and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then executes each shard group via runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), which now maps the same targets through applyTemplateVariables() again at this line.
