The Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 (and the same change in account/messages_lt.properties totpStep1) was replaced with 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see instructions in the wrong language on the TOTP setup screens; the previous Lithuanian text that contained the illegal anchors should have been translated/adapted, not replaced with the Italian string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify Italian text incorrectly used in messages_lt.properties, where Lithuanian translation is required.

false_positives.candidate:
MessageFormat choice syntax breaks JS i18next interpolation

error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from the JS UI convention 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to Java MessageFormat syntax 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. Every other placeholder in this account-ui file (and in js/apps/admin-ui messages_en.properties, changed the same way) uses {{n}} for the React/i18next renderer, which does not evaluate {n,choice,...}; users in the account/admin consoles will see the raw placeholders/choice expression instead of the interpolated counts. The choice/plural form is only valid for the server-side themes properties.

Missing English counterpart crashes verifier instead of reporting a verification error

verifySafeHtml() derives the English file purely by string replacement on the absolute path and throws RuntimeException('unable to read file ...') when that derived file does not exist. verify() only catches IOException and converts it to MojoExecutionException, so a locale file whose English source lives elsewhere or whose name does not match the '_xx.properties' -> '_en.properties' pattern (e.g. a messages.properties without locale suffix, or a new theme location) aborts the whole plugin run with an unhandled stack trace instead of producing a collected verification message or a clear Mojo failure.

HTML allowance is keyed only to presence of any HTML in English, not the tags actually used

containsHtml() returns true if the English value contains any '<[a-z]+...>' tag, and then POLICY_SOME_HTML unconditionally allows br/p/strong/b in the translation even if the English string used none of them (for example an English value containing only an <a> anchor, which is stripped by santizeAnchors). Conversely, legitimate English markup outside br/p/strong/b/a is rejected in translations even when copied verbatim. This makes the check both permissive for injected formatting tags not present in the source and prone to false positives, weakening the stated guarantee that only HTML present in the English source may appear in translations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

Line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") instead of requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...). A null rawTokenId therefore passes construction and produces a token id ending in ':null' from encodeTokenId(), instead of failing fast as the message intends.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same constructor validation bug: grantType is checked twice while rawTokenId is never checked, allowing null rawTokenId values through.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher is inverted and off-by-one

The encoded prefix is 2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type, so the grant shortcut is substring(4,6), not substring(3,5). The matcher also returns false when substring equals expectedGrantShortcut and otherwise does not reject a mismatching grant at all. Consequently expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken will fail for correct tokens and pass for wrong grant types, masking regressions. It should be: if (!items[0].substring(4,6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false; (with a length guard to avoid StringIndexOutOfBounds).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both defects described by the golden comment: the grant shortcut should use substring(4,6), and matching the expected shortcut should permit success with the UUID check rather than return false.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks all custom grant-type factories

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an SPI implemented by out-of-tree/custom grant types. Adding getShortcut() as an abstract interface method means every existing custom factory no longer compiles and, if deployed as an old binary, throws AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates provider factories. This is a breaking SPI change for a feature that could degrade gracefully. The method should be a default method (e.g. returning the unknown shortcut) so existing grants continue to work.

Copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context removed and constructor can now NPE

The public Context(Context) copy constructor is deleted, breaking any grant implementation that cloned/modified the context before processing. In addition the remaining constructor now unconditionally calls formParams.getFirst(GRANT_TYPE), so code that constructed a Context with null formParams (previously valid) now throws NullPointerException at construction. Both changes break external grant types without a deprecation path.

Token issuance now fails for unknown or unregistered grant types

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() copies the raw GRANT_TYPE attribute into AccessTokenContext, and encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException if that string has no registered shortcut. TokenManager.initToken() now calls this for every access token, so any flow or custom grant that sets a grant_type value that is not exactly a registered OAuth2GrantType factory id (or a custom provider returning a null/duplicate shortcut, which also causes a ConcurrentHashMap NPE in the factory refresh path) will fail token creation with a 500 instead of issuing a token. Previously such tokens were issued with a plain UUID. Encoding should fall back to the 'na' unknown shortcut rather than aborting issuance.

Lightweight-token detection uses ambient context client and can NPE or misclassify

getShouldUseLightweightToken(session) reads session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(...) (AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper line 86) and does not use the client from clientSessionContext. TokenManager.initToken() is invoked from flows where the KeycloakContext client is not set or differs from the client session's client (e.g. internally created/exchanged tokens), so this can throw NullPointerException during initToken or encode 'lt'/'rt' based on the wrong client. The client should be taken from clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient() and null-checked.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw recovery codes are handed to and persisted by user storage in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the generatedCodes list (the raw, human-usable recovery codes) as JSON and passes it as the UserCredentialModel challenge response to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Unlike the local path, which stores RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel data containing hashes of the codes, a user-storage provider that persists this input verbatim (as the PR's own BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at updateCredential/getCredentials) ends up storing all unused recovery codes in plaintext at rest. Anyone with read access to the external store then obtains valid second-factor bypass codes for the user. The codes should be hashed before leaving Keycloak, or the storage contract must require and document hashing, so federated persistence is not weaker than local persistence.

Federated recovery codes are never consumed or removed after successful use

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, the code only checks recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the model returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() and calls removeStoredCredentialById() when exhausted. For a federated credential this does not work: consumption/marking-used is performed by the local RecoveryAuthnCodes credential provider when it updates its stored credential, whereas a user-storage validator (such as the PR's BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(), which only compares the input against the stored list) does not mutate the stored codes, so allCodesUsed() stays false and the same code remains replayable indefinitely. Additionally removeStoredCredentialById() removes local DB credentials by id and cannot delete a credential held in user storage (federated credentials must be disabled/updated via the storage provider), so even an exhausted federated credential is not removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES regeneration path can be bypassed. Single-use semantics for recovery codes are therefore broken for federated users.

getCredential prefers federated over local without aligning with validation, risking wrong code state when both exist

getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if any exists and only falls back to the locally stored credential otherwise. This helper now drives both the login form's next-code number (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) and the post-login allCodesUsed()/removal decision (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), but credential validation through credentialManager().isValid() can be satisfied by the local credential provider. For a user who has both a stale local credential and a federated one (e.g. codes created locally before the storage started supporting the type, and then re-created in storage via the new fallback logic in CredentialHelper), the UI will prompt for the code number from the federated set and exhaustion will be evaluated against the federated set, while validation/consumption may act on the local set. The result is a wrong requested code index and failure to regenerate/remove the credential that was actually consumed. Lookup precedence must match the validator's precedence, or dual credentials must be prevented/deduplicated.

getCredentials dereferences MyUser without the null check used by sibling methods

The new getCredentials() does var myUser = getMyUser(user); and immediately accesses myUser.recoveryCodes (line 235) and myUser.otp (line 247). getMyUser() returns users.get(...), which is null for a username not present in the map, and sibling methods such as isConfiguredFor() and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() explicitly guard against that. If credential listing is invoked for a user not in this storage's map, the provider throws NullPointerException instead of returning an empty credential stream, breaking credential listing/account flows for such users.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled gating is only tested for metadata and its exit code is not asserted

The new test covers only `update-compatibility metadata` without `--features=rolling-updates` and only asserts the error message. It does not cover the separately added gating in `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` and does not assert exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`) for either subcommand. A regression that leaves `check` ungated, or returns the picocli software/usage error codes instead of 4, would therefore pass while breaking scripts and the operator flow that rely on distinguishing feature-disabled from recreate (3) and rolling (0).

Caution overstates that the operator will fail without rolling-updates

The new caution says that while in preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled, otherwise the Keycloak Operator will fail. That is not scoped to using `spec.update.strategy`, and it contradicts the PR's own operator test setup in UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment, where the default/null-strategy deployment returns before enabling `rolling-updates` and is still expected to deploy and upgrade. As written, users with ordinary CRs will believe every deployment must enable a preview feature or the operator fails; the text should be limited to deployments that use the update-strategy feature.

Exit code 4 is described as a compatibility verdict although no check ran

The table describes exit code 4 as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible' when the feature is disabled. In that case UpdateCompatibilityCheck and UpdateCompatibilityMetadata return before validating/reading metadata or computing compatibility, so compatibility is unknown rather than disproven. Scripts following this wording may permanently choose a recreate/downtime path for a merely misconfigured invocation instead of treating 4 as an enablement/configuration error distinct from the recreate verdict (3).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing all-clients resource causes NullPointerException during evaluation

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no instance resource exists the code loads the all-clients resource via getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls findByResource(server, resource) and later builds a ResourcePermission from it without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the 'Clients' resource is absent (for example in realms whose admin-permissions client was initialized before the Clients type existed, since init() returns early when the client already exists and never adds the new scopes/resources). Permission checks for such realms then throw NullPointerException instead of denying permission or lazily creating the type resource.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission: getResourceTypeResource can return null, which is passed to findByResource without a defensive null check and causes a NullPointerException.

false_positives.candidate:
Role-mapping checks lose manage/admin fallback

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only evaluate the corresponding fine-grained scope for the client. They do not fall back to canManage(client), unlike the V1 evaluator where an administrator who can manage a client (including via the manage-clients admin role) can map its roles. A full realm admin or a user granted only the Clients 'manage' scope is therefore incorrectly forbidden from role/composite/client-scope role mapping in V2.

Resource display name is not resolved for Clients resources

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the type resource and resolves instance resources to usernames. Clients resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), but instance resources created by getOrCreateResource are named by client id and have no display name set, and the 'Clients' type resource is not translated to 'All clients'. Permission/resource representations for Clients will consequently expose a null/blank name instead of the client id or 'All clients'.

Removal listener can dispatch to V2 evaluator that throws on cleanup

The listener now runs whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but management() dispatches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is also enabled. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so when both features are enabled, role/client/group removal events invoke V2 cleanup and fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of disabling permissions. The guard needs to exclude the V2 case (or the dispatch needs to use the V1 evaluator for this cleanup).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage to holders of only the view scope

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the 'view' scope on all Groups passes canManage(). requireManage() is based on this method and is used e.g. by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup to create top-level groups, so a view-only FGAP admin can create groups (and perform other operations gated only by requireManage()). canManage() should require only the MANAGE scope, as canManage(GroupModel) on line 79 already does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same scope-check bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): accepting VIEW or MANAGE permits view-only users to perform manage/write operations, whereas this method should require MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs/names

Resources for Groups are looked up by name, where the resource name is the group ID (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and hasPermission(String) does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)). Here the code passes groupResource.getId() (the authorization resource's own UUID) to hasPermission, so findByName misses and evaluation falls back to the all-Groups resource, ignoring per-group view-members/manage-members grants. It then adds groupResource.getId() to the result, but callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser/getUsersCount and BruteForceUsersResource expect actual group IDs for the UserModel.GROUPS filter. Consequently admins with per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS see no group members in user searches/counts. Both places should use groupResource.getName().
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same resource-ID versus underlying group-ID mismatch in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: passing authorization resource IDs to name-based permission lookup and returning those IDs for group filtering/counts. Both propose using resource names to align with actual group IDs and the evaluator contract.

false_positives.candidate:
getResourceName has no handling for the new Groups resource type

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users resource type, returning the username for a user resource and 'All users' for the type resource. For the newly added Groups type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), but group resources created by getOrCreateResource have the group ID as their name and no display name set, so permission listings for group resources will show a null/blank or raw ID instead of the group name (and no 'All groups' label). Add the analogous Groups branch resolving the group by resource name and returning its name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle

The method contract in CryptoProvider is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) security provider, and callers use it for BC-specific algorithms and provider names. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a stock JDK is typically the SUN provider, not BouncyCastle. Any authz-client code path (or synced keycloak-client code path) that consults getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC capabilities will get the wrong provider and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider or behave differently. It should return null like WildFlyElytronProvider if no BC provider is available, or an actually-registered BC provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside this repository (custom server providers, downstream Elytron/FIPS variants, test doubles) will fail to compile and, if compiled against the old interface, throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts providers by order(). This should be a default method (e.g. returning a defined default priority) so existing providers keep working and only providers needing precedence override it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it. The candidate adds failure modes and a suggested default-method fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now silently chosen non-deterministically instead of failing fast

Previously detectProvider() threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. Now it sorts by order() descending and silently ignores the rest, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200. If two of those are co-present (e.g. default + Elytron in WildFly, or default + FIPS), the winner depends only on unspecified ServiceLoader iteration order among equal keys, so a non-FIPS provider could be selected in FIPS mode or vice versa with only a debug log. Equal top orders should either retain the fail-fast error or have a deterministic, documented tie-break.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and only assert round-trip equality

The shared constructor creates one KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() key, which defaults to a 256-bit curve, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. asn1derToConcatenatedRS merely zero-pads/truncates r and s to algorithm.getSignatureLength()/2, so the round-trip assertion passes for ES384/ES512 even though no P-384/P-521 key or real signature of that size is ever produced or verified. The test never verifies the produced DER signature with Signature.verify(), so conversion defects for larger curves or leading-zero r/s values would go undetected. Each algorithm should generate a key on its matching curve and verify the converted signature cryptographically.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, making the concurrency assertion racy and leaking the thread

The test starts a reader thread at line 139 that loops while deletedAll is false, sets deletedAll to true at line 155, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty at line 157 without joining the thread. A request already in flight can still fail and add to caughtExceptions after the assertion, so a real concurrent-access failure can be missed and the test can pass spuriously. Conversely the unjoined busy-loop thread can outlive the test, continue issuing admin requests against a realm/client being torn down or reused, and pollute subsequent tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the test sets deletedAll and immediately checks caughtExceptions without waiting for the reader thread, allowing an in-flight request to add an exception after the assertion. The candidate's additional thread-leak concern does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the other lazy-delegate methods

The fix null-checks only getSubGroupsCount() at line 275, but getSubGroupsStream(String,Integer,Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer,Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String,Boolean,Integer,Integer) at line 268 still dereference modelSupplier.get() without a null check. If the group is deleted concurrently, the delegate lookup returns null exactly as in getSubGroupsCount(), so these methods throw NullPointerException instead of handling the deleted group. The reported concurrent-access NPE therefore remains reachable through subgroup listing/search, not just subgroup counting.

Unthrottled reader loop can overwhelm the test server and collect unbounded failures

The reader thread at lines 140-149 spins with no pause, repeatedly requesting all groups with Integer.MAX_VALUE results while 100 groups are deleted, and appends every exception to an unbounded CopyOnWriteArrayList. Depending on timing/machine speed this can hammer the server and admin-client token endpoint enough to create timing-dependent failures or resource pressure unrelated to the bug under test, making the regression test flaky rather than a deterministic check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at line 160. There is no no-arg overload, so services module fails to compile and none of the PR can be built or tested. The call should pass context.getUser().
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing required UserModel argument in the call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() within UsernameForm.authenticate().

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys are now disabled for unauthenticated (ID-less) login

authenticate() previously called webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) when context.getUser() was null, which sets the WebAuthn challenge/RP attributes needed for discoverable-passkey (ID-less) login on the initial username/password page. The new code only calls it when isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) is true, and that helper at lines 160-162 requires user != null. Consequently first-time/anonymous login pages get no challenge and no conditional-UI webauthn form, breaking passkey login for users not yet identified (existing tests such as webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey in PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest expect the webauth form on the initial page). The helper should not require a non-null user; fillContextForm is already made safe for an identified user by WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() returning false.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same null-user guard preventing authenticate() from calling fillContextForm on the initial login page, leaving conditional passkey UI uninitialized and breaking ID-less passkey authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are never killed before being replaced

Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess objects are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the fork-context Process class). The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard therefore evaluates to False for every real flusher process. When _ensure_processes_alive detects a hang (is_alive() is True but healthy_since is stale), it skips process.kill() and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards. The hung process keeps running alongside its replacement, so two processes can concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produce for the same Redis shards, risking duplicate or racing segment flushes, while the hung process continues consuming resources. The guard should check against the spawn context's process type / BaseProcess, or duck-type on kill/terminate.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: spawn-context flusher processes fail the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check, causing hung processes to skip termination. The candidate adds consequences and potential fixes without changing the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
join() never terminates spawned flusher processes

join() uses the same isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check before calling process.terminate(). Because the flushers are SpawnProcess objects from the spawn context, this check is always False in production, so any flusher that does not exit promptly after stopped is set is never terminated. join() waits until the deadline for each process in sequence and then silently returns with daemon processes still alive, leaking processes and potentially leaving flushers running against Redis/Kafka after the consumer strategy has shut down. Use the mp_context process base type or hasattr-based termination instead.

Negative or zero flusher-process configuration crashes or disables flushing

The CLI option --flusher-processes accepts any int with no validation. On Arroyo partition revocation/rebalance this abandons in-flight messages, and because the same pool is shared (see result_consumer factory), closing one strategy instance also kills the pool for any subsequently created strategy: queue.put then raises queue.ShutDown, which submit()'s catch-all converts into add+complete offset, silently committing unprocessed messages.

Catch-all in submit marks offsets complete for messages never enqueued

submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except and, on any exception, adds and immediately completes the offset. This conflates poison messages with transient failures: e.g. grouping_fn raising, queue shutdown raising queue.ShutDown, or the real decode_payload asserting on FilteredPayload (decode_payload asserts payload is not FilteredPayload) all cause the offset to become committable even though nothing was processed, silently dropping the message with only a log line.

_commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls commit_function (the Arroyo Commit callable supplied to create_with_partitions) from there. Arroyo processing strategies are driven single-threaded by StreamProcessor and the commit callable/consumer commit path is not documented as thread-safe; invoking it concurrently with the main consumer loop risks races with the processor's own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit logic and with partition assignment changes, potentially committing offsets for partitions no longer owned.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(group_key) % num_queues. For str keys hash() is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the 'consistent hashing' claimed in the docstring is not stable across restarts or across consumer processes: the same subscription is assigned to a different queue whenever the process restarts, breaking the ordering/affinity guarantee the pool exists to provide relative to any other process or previous incarnation. A stable digest (e.g. md5/sha like other Sentry grouping code) is required.

Committable-offset scan is O(offset range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) and is invoked every second by the commit loop. When one slow item blocks a partition (the exact scenario this PR targets), the outstanding window grows with throughput, so each scan walks an ever-larger range of integers doing two set lookups per offset, and all_offsets keeps every uncommitted offset in memory. A single stuck subscription can thus make commit processing progressively more expensive and delay commits for all partitions.

Queue pool and offset tracker are never reset on partition reassignment

The FixedQueuePool (and its OffsetTracker) is created once in the factory __init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. OffsetTracker state (all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed) is keyed only by Partition and is never cleared when partitions are revoked or reassigned, and last_committed starts at -1 regardless of the committed position Arroyo passes in the partitions mapping. After a rebalance, stale outstanding entries from the previous assignment can permanently block commits for a reassigned partition, or stale last_committed state can cause incorrect committable calculations for a partition this consumer no longer owns or newly owns at a different position.

Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify which spans `zpopmin` evicts (including whether the root/segment span can be evicted, invalidating `has_root_span` flushing), nothing verifies ordering by differing `end_timestamp_precise` scores after `zunionstore` merges, and nothing covers redirect chains over 1000 hops. false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset (which the dashboard-widget split logic can change to discover or keep as the metrics dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead of scoped_dataset. When a metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced request is split into a Discover error query, upsampling is wrongly skipped; conversely a transaction-like split can be transformed based on the original dataset even though the executed dataset/query is not error data. The transform decision must be made for the dataset actually executed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: upsampling eligibility checks the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing upsampling to be skipped when a metrics request is split into a Discover query.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count is only registered on Discover but is generated for the errors dataset

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count() whenever _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True, and that helper returns True unconditionally for the errors dataset. However the new SnQLFunction is only added to the Discover dataset's function_converter; the errors dataset has its own function converter without upsampled_count. Any events-stats request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore fail query validation/building (unknown function) instead of returning upsampled counts.

Substring check treats negated error filters as error-focused queries

_is_error_focused_query does a raw substring search for 'event.type:error', so queries such as '!event.type:error', '-event.type:error', or 'event.type:transaction OR !event.type:error' are classified as error-focused. The endpoint will then rewrite count() to sum(sample_weight) over predominantly transaction/non-error rows, where sample_weight is not meaningful/populated, returning zero or badly undercounted series instead of the real count.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no fallback for rows whose sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects will normally contain historical events and events ingested without client sampling information; ClickHouse sum() ignores NULLs (and yields NULL/0 for an all-NULL bucket), so those events silently disappear from upsampled counts rather than counting as 1 each. A safe aggregate needs a per-row default such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

Cache key relies on Python hash() and the invalidation helper is never wired up

Eligibility is cached under a key built from hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) and invalidate_upsampling_cache recomputes the same expression, but no code path calls invalidate_upsampling_cache when the project allowlist option changes. Combined with hash-collision risk between different project sets, one project set can briefly serve another set's cached eligibility and, more importantly, allowlist removals keep upsampling (and additions keep not upsampling) until TTL expiry with no invalidation hook despite the helper suggesting otherwise. Use a deterministic, collision-resistant key (e.g. the joined project ids) and either call invalidation on option change or remove the dead helper.

Accidental gitlink/subproject file committed

This adds a file `sentry-repo` containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a', i.e. an accidental nested-repository gitlink. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, will confuse tooling/checkouts, and should be removed before merge.

Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query inspects request.GET['query'], but _get_event_stats executes the `query` argument passed through get_event_stats_data and the dashboard split logic, which can differ from the raw GET parameter (split code appends 'AND !event.type:transaction', callers can supply modified queries). Eligibility can therefore be decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, causing missed upsampling for split error queries or transforms applied to non-error executions. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility check instead of re-reading the request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the permission-cache key prefix

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping/length-prefixing, so distinct tuples such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key; Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource. The key also uses the same 'perm_<uid>_<action>' prefix as userPermCacheKey in the same underlying cache, so crafted/extended components can collide with a permission entry (bool vs map JSON), causing spurious cache misses/corrupt entries.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same ambiguous underscore-concatenated denial cache keys, including a concrete collision example and the resulting incorrect permission denials. Its additional concern about permission-cache prefix overlap does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache prevents newly granted/created resources from becoming accessible until TTL expiry

Check returns Allowed:false solely from permDenialCache before consulting fresh DB permissions, and no path clears a denial entry when permissions change or when getIdentityPermissions later refreshes permCache for another request. A user checked before creating/being granted a dashboard or folder (or before a grant propagates) is therefore still denied for the full shortCacheTTL (30s), partially defeating this PR's goal of letting creators immediately fetch newly created resources. Only TTL expiry unblocks them.

Denial is cached even when the denial may be caused by a stale folder tree

On the DB-recheck path, checkPermission -> checkInheritedPermissions still uses buildFolderTree's folderCache (30s TTL); permissions are refreshed but the folder hierarchy is not. A dashboard in a newly created/moved folder can thus be denied because ancestors are missing from the stale tree, and line 154 then promotes that possibly-stale result into permDenialCache for another TTL, extending the incorrect denial beyond the folder-cache expiry and making it immune to the permission refresh.

List still returns stale cached permissions with no revalidation

List accepts getCachedIdentityPermissions as authoritative whenever present and never re-queries the DB, unlike Check which falls back when the cached set does not contain the requested resource. A newly created dashboard/folder (or newly granted scope) will therefore be omitted from List results until permCache expires, so the PR's stated fix for fetching newly created dashboards/folders does not work for list/fetch-many flows that rely on List.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled KeyError

integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes every pre-existing Integration row has a sender dict with a login. Integrations created before sender was recorded (or created without that metadata) have no such key, so re-adding such an installation to an organization after its OrganizationIntegration was removed raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the graceful github-integration-failed page or a completed install. The lookup should use .get() chaining and decide explicitly how to handle absent sender data.

false_positives.candidate:

When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch immediately calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state github_authenticated_user against the installer/sender. The sender is only available from the webhook-created Integration, so this path is taken whenever the GitHub installation webhook has not yet created the Integration (a normal race between the install redirect and webhook delivery, and the path used by the ordinary fresh-install flow in the tests). An attacker who installed the app can therefore complete linking from a different authenticated GitHub account simply by finishing the pipeline before the webhook creates the row, defeating the validation this PR adds.

If GitHub's access-token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or returns an HTTP error that safe_urlopen raises for, the exception propagates out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and produces a 500 rather than the 'Invalid installation request' failure page promised for bad/reused codes and token failures. get_user_info() on line 434 has the same unhandled-failure exposure for the subsequent /user call.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The rewritten test_installation_not_found supplies a deliberately wrong state (ddd023...) on the second request, so OAuthLoginView rejects it for state mismatch and asserts 'Invalid installation request.' The request never reaches GitHubInstallation/build_integration, so the stubbed 404 from GET /app/installations/{id} and the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' IntegrationError path are no longer exercised despite the test name; a regression in 404 handling would pass unnoticed.

OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering

The cached branch collects identity-provider IDs and then the matching models into a HashSet and returns identityProviders.stream(). HashSet iteration order is unspecified and unrelated to the JPA delegate's ordering, so callers of getForLogin that consume the stream in order (e.g. take the first matching broker) can now observe a different, unstable provider order compared with the uncached path. Preserve encounter order (e.g. LinkedHashSet / ordered list) when materialising the cached IDs.

Login-cache update check compares an organization-aware original against a raw updated model

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is called from update() with 'original' obtained via getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): its isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization is disabled. The 'updated' model is the raw caller-supplied model whose isEnabled() only reflects the IdP flag, while the JPA getForLogin query that built the cache also only checks the IdP enabled flag. For an IdP in a disabled organization that is enabled/public (so its ID is in the cached login list), an update that sets hideOnLogin/linkOnly therefore yields predicate(original)=false and predicate(updated)=false and skips invalidation, leaving the now-hidden/link-only IdP's ID in the cached login list; callers such as OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-check isEnabled, so it can still be offered on the login page. Compute the original predicate from the unwrapped stored model (or the same semantics as the JPA query) before deciding to skip invalidation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.
Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is dead, inverted logic that always returns false

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false in the if branch and false unconditionally afterwards, so the feature-flag check has no effect and the function name/contract is misleading. The current behavior (always disabled) matches the PR intent, but a future maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions behind the flag will find flipping the toggle does nothing and may 'fix' the wrong branch, accidentally re-enabling it insecurely. Make the disable explicit (e.g. return false with a comment referencing the CVE/removal, or delete the helper and inline the rejection) instead of leaving inverted dead logic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the feature flag, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions. The candidate's additional discussion of intent and remediation does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command construction bypasses the new disabled check

UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled; only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in reader.go has the new gate. This legacy entry point is therefore protected only indirectly because the stub DB makes sql.TablesList fail, returning a misleading BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' instead of an explicit disabled/not-implemented rejection. If the DuckDB-backed DB implementation is restored or replaced, this path will silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 surface without passing through the reader check. Gate both construction paths (or remove/stub UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand) so disabling does not depend on a downstream stub error.

No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected even with the feature flag on

This is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI via DuckDB SQL expressions), but the PR adds no test asserting that a QueryTypeSQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path cannot execute SQL. Without such a test, restoring the go-duck dependency or simplifying enableSqlExpressions back to a plain flag check would reintroduce the vulnerability with no failing test. Add tests covering both entry points with the flag on and off.

go.work.sum churn is inconsistent with the go.mod/go.sum dependency removal

go.mod/go.sum drop go-duck and its transitive deps (apache/thrift, klauspost/asmfmt, minio/asm2plan9s, minio/c2goasm, JohnCGriffin/overflow), yet go.work.sum re-adds hashes for several of those same modules while dropping unrelated ones (Azure azblob, google go-replayers). This suggests the workspace sums were not regenerated with go work sync after the removal and may fail verification or resurrect the removed DuckDB transitive graph for other workspace modules. Regenerate and verify go.work.sum so the vulnerable dependency is actually gone from the whole workspace, not just the main module.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check under write lock causes duplicate loads and cache replacement

After acquiring the exclusive Lock at line 48, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. Two concurrent cold-cache callers in non-Dev mode can both pass the RLock check with ret==nil, then sequentially each perform readWebAssetsFromFile (and SetContentDeliveryURL) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache, with the first caller returning a pointer that is no longer the cached one. This wastes I/O and can yield different EntryPointAssets instances to concurrent callers; re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after Lock and returning it would make the fast path race-free and single-load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: GetWebAssets checks the cache under a read lock but fails to re-check it after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate and overwrite the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Mutex only guards the pointer, shared mutable EntryPointAssets is still returned to all callers

GetWebAssets returns the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer stored in the global cache to every caller. The new RWMutex protects only reading/writing the pointer variable, not the pointed-to struct/slices. Any caller that mutates the returned value (as this function itself does via result.SetContentDeliveryURL at line 64) races with concurrent readers of the cached object. The fix is incomplete unless callers are guaranteed never to mutate the result; returning a copy/clone on the cached path (or documenting/enforcing immutability) is needed to fully eliminate the shared-global-state race described in the PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log 'Annotations/Tags to clean' and 'cleaned ...' via r.log.Error on every batch, including successful batches where err is nil. This will emit error-level logs (often wired to alerting/error reporting) for normal operation and each message embeds the full ids slice, which can be tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes, creating huge noisy log lines. These should be Debug/Info level without dumping all IDs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine debugging or progress information being logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend Debug or Info instead. The candidate's concern about full ID lists is additional detail that does not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval reduced 10x without justification

The global cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations) now runs 10x more often, not just annotation cleanup. This unrelated change increases DB and filesystem load on all Grafana instances and partially works against the goal of reducing MySQL contention from annotation cleanup. It should be reverted or justified and scoped to annotations only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute as a concern because more frequent cleanup can increase database load and contention. The candidate adds scope and mitigation details but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

For SQLite with a large batch size, deleteByIDs builds the IN (...) list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop over all ids. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a 32767-ID list (as exercised by the new test) is O(n^2) in bytes copied and can take seconds and large allocations before the DELETE runs. Use strings.Builder (already imported) to build the list linearly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures and DeleteCollection legacy result are recorded against the wrong metric

On Storage.Create failure (line 45) and Storage.Update failure (line 129) the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage) even though legacy was never attempted, so storage errors pollute the legacy latency/error series and no storage error is recorded. In DeleteCollection the async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency is counted as storage latency. Delete success at line 106 also passes `name` in place of the kind used by every other call, creating inconsistent/high-cardinality metric labels. This makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies Delete success passing `name` instead of the kind used by other metric calls, matching the golden comment's inconsistency with `options.Kind`. The additional metric-recording issues do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled

Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) derive the legacy timeout context from ctx, which is the incoming request context embedded with the logger. The Kubernetes API handler cancels that context when the request returns, and Mode 3 returns immediately after spawning the goroutine. The legacy operation therefore races request completion and will often receive context.Canceled before writing, silently defeating the stated safety copy to legacy storage. The goroutine should derive from a detached context (for example context.WithoutCancel or a background context, preserving needed values) before applying the 10-second timeout.

Async Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object already written to unified storage

Storage.Update has already consumed objInfo to compute the updated object from the unified-storage version. The goroutine then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update, which will fetch the legacy (different) old object and call UpdatedObject again. That second computation can carry the unified-storage ResourceVersion/UID state and fail optimistic-concurrency or validation against legacy, or produce different content than what was committed to unified storage. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in updateWrapper carrying the exact object returned by Storage.Update; dropping that wrapper is a regression for the dual-write update path.

Async Create passes the storage-mutated input object to legacy Create

d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...) is commonly implemented by mutating the passed-in obj in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, creation timestamp, generated name). The goroutine then passes that same obj to d.Legacy.Create. Legacy create can therefore see a non-empty ResourceVersion/UID and reject the create, or create a legacy record whose identity/RV does not match a fresh create. Legacy should receive a copy cleared/derived from the returned created object (as other dual-writer modes do by stripping ResourceVersion), and doing the copy after Storage.Create also needs to happen before the caller can mutate the returned object.

Legacy async failures are never logged and a legacy panic crashes the process

All four async legacy goroutines only record a duration metric: the returned error is never logged (and in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection there is not even a log line naming the object on failure), and there is no recover. Because mode 3 promises legacy is written 'just as a safe measure', an operator cannot discover from logs that the safety copy is failing, and a panic in Legacy storage code inside the detached goroutine is not recovered by the HTTP handler middleware and will crash the server process.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes and share one mock for both stores

The tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock around the same *mock.Mock, so a call to either store satisfies indistinguishable expectations, and they never call AssertExpectations / AssertCalled for the legacy Create, Update or Delete paths (Delete/DeleteCollection tests do not even register legacy expectations). Because the legacy calls now run in unsynchronized goroutines, the tests pass even if legacy is never written, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with subsequent tests reusing the package-level example objects/mock state. The async behaviour (legacy called, with what object, within the timeout) is the core feature of mode 3 and needs synchronised assertions (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup in the mock).

New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility and are racy

The new file/unified mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy API (getFromBothAPIs and the legacy list/search checks). Under the new implementation the legacy write is fire-and-forget with a 10-second window, so there is no happens-before guarantee when those legacy assertions run; the test will be flaky and can also pass spuriously if a later assertion happens to be late enough. The mode 3 integration case needs polling/eventual-consistency assertions for the legacy side (or to wait for the async write) rather than the synchronous checks used for modes 1/2.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

canDelete is now OR-computed from the Grafana prom-rule abilities so it can be true when only promRule is supplied (the new list view passes no rulerRule after GrafanaRuleLoader was removed), but rendering is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In GrafanaRuleListItem/RuleActionsButtons.V2 only promRule is passed, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete is never rendered for Grafana rules in the list view, even for users with delete permission. The same pattern breaks Pause at line 123 (`canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...`), so paused-state toggling is also unreachable there.

Shard-split queries are interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery() already maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) because it needs the interpolated selector to fetch __stream_shard__ values, and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then executes each shard group via runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), which now maps the same targets through applyTemplateVariables() again at this line. Template replacement is therefore applied twice to every sharded query (the updated shard test even expects 5 calls for 1 target: 1 up-front plus 1 per shard sub-request). This is not guaranteed idempotent: applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters (adhoc filters) into the expr, so the second pass can duplicate label matchers/line filters in the LogQL sent to Loki (duplicate matchers in a stream selector can be rejected), and variable values introduced by the first pass that contain '$...' sequences can be re-expanded against the sub-request. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Limit check and insert are not atomic, so concurrent devices can exceed the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then, in a separate DB session, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Two or more concurrent first-time devices (especially from different Grafana instances, whose local caches are per-process) can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. in a transaction/lock or a single conditional statement) if it is meant to be a hard cap.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both suggest enforcing the check and insert atomically using a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Rejected device is cached as tagged and bypasses the limit on retry

As written, order(0) would be invalid/dropped and ordered items are shifted one group toward unordered items, so the legacy-prefixed rendering this mixin exists for (used by .panel order(3) in header.scss and .extra-info-wrapper order(2) in topic.scss) can order header children differently from the standard `order` rendering.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: legacy -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require 1-based values, so copying $val directly makes order(0) invalid and can cause incorrect layout in older browsers.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex .small-action loses the right-aligned action button
