true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing ? so it is never used

ActiveModelSerializers in this codebase gates attributes with methods named `include_<attr>?`, as seen in include_email?, include_card_image_badge_id?, include_stats? and the methods generated by untrusted_attributes. The new method is defined as `include_website_name` without `?`, so the serializer will never call it. Consequently website_name is serialized even when website is blank (as a nil value), and the intended present? check provides no protection; the method must be renamed to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same primary issue: include_website_name lacks the required ? suffix, preventing the serializer from using it for conditional inclusion. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the main bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not hidden for untrusted TL0 users viewed anonymously

`website` is listed in untrusted_attributes so it is suppressed when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object) applies (TL0 user seen by anonymous, to prevent spam/abuse harvesting), but the newly added `website_name` attribute at line 43 is not added to that list (lines 105-111) and has no equivalent restriction check. Anonymous visitors therefore still receive the website host and, for same-domain sites, the full path derived directly from the hidden website field, defeating the existing restriction. website_name should be added to untrusted_attributes (or otherwise gated the same way), and the spec's untrusted_attributes list should cover it.

Displayed website_name drops query string and fragment, so 'complete URL' text can be incomplete/misleading

When the website host matches the instance host, the code returns `website_host + URI(website).path` only. For a website such as http://example.com/?page=user or http://example.com/profile#section the display text becomes just `example.com/` / `example.com/profile`, omitting the query/fragment that distinguish the actual target while the link still points to the full URL. The visible label therefore does not show the complete URL as the PR title promises; query (and fragment) should be appended when present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of origin equality

The handler accepts a message whenever discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) !== -1, i.e. whenever the sender's origin is any substring of the configured Discourse URL, rather than requiring e.origin to equal the Discourse origin. Origins that are prefixes/substrings of the configured URL are accepted, weakening the check that the resize message actually came from the Discourse embed iframe; the origin should be parsed once and compared exactly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same security flaw: using indexOf substring matching for postMessage origin validation allows unintended origins to pass instead of requiring exact origin equality. The differing bypass examples do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Full referer URL used as postMessage targetOrigin never matches

postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin (scheme://host:port), but this passes the entire request.referer including its path and query. Browsers compare it against the parent window's origin, so the discourse-resize message is silently never delivered and the embed iframe added by embed.js never gets resized to its content height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing the full referrer URL instead of just its origin as postMessage's targetOrigin prevents delivery of the resize message and stops the iframe from resizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content

i.content is nil for RSS/Atom items that only provide a summary/description (SimpleRSS does not guarantee content), so i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError and aborts the whole hourly poll, preventing all remaining items from being imported. String#scrub also does not exist on the Ruby 1.9/2.0 runtimes this codebase targets, so this raises NoMethodError even when content is present.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: feed items may lack content, so calling i.content.scrub on nil raises NoMethodError and crashes polling. Its additional Ruby compatibility concern does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript

request.referer is inserted verbatim inside a single-quoted JS string passed to postMessage. The controller only checks the referer's host, so a referer such as http://<embeddable_host>/'-alert(1)-' contains a quote that breaks out of the string and executes arbitrary script in the embed page on the Discourse origin. The referer must be JS/HTML-escaped (and reduced to an origin) before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious header content to break out of the string and execute arbitrary scripts.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import stores attacker-controlled RSS/Atom or scraped page contents as a Post with cook_method raw_html. Post#cook returns raw verbatim for that method, and the cooked HTML is rendered raw in topic and embed views. No sanitization is applied on this path (PollFeed passes feed content straight through), so a feed item or embedded page containing <script>/event-handler markup becomes stored XSS for every forum visitor who views the imported topic.

Unauthenticated requests can flood the retrieve_topic job queue

Every GET for an unknown embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job. The 60-second throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieve, which only runs when a job is executed, not before enqueueing. Anyone who can present the embeddable referer can therefore issue many requests for distinct or identical URLs faster than jobs drain and fill Sidekiq with jobs that each may fetch remote pages/feed content, instead of throttling/deduplicating at enqueue time.

Spec expects synchronous TopicRetriever use that the controller no longer performs

This test expects TopicRetriever.new/retrieve to be called during EmbedController#best, but the controller instead calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). The mock expectations can never be satisfied by the implementation under test, so this example fails and provides no coverage of the actual enqueued job arguments (user_id and embed_url).

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with no validation

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url) on the supplied URL before TopicEmbed.import's scheme check runs, and performs no host allowlist, private-address, or redirect validation. Callers that pass externally influenced URLs (e.g. thread links from a Disqus export) can make the server issue requests to internal/metadata addresses (SSRF) and import the response. Host validation in TopicRetriever does not protect this entry point.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `downsize` definition silently overwrites the first in Ruby

Ruby does not support method overloading: defining `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined at line 145. Any existing caller passing separate width and height (5 positional arguments including opts) will now raise ArgumentError, breaking thumbnail/downsize paths that use the old signature. The two signatures must be merged into one method that handles both forms.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the second downsize definition overrides the first, making the separate width/height signature unavailable and breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores configured per-type size settings

Replacing `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a constant `10 * 1024` breaks the admin-configured contract for both images and attachments: sites that lowered `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` will now accept files client-side that the server/model then rejects (or expensively downsizes), and sites that raised the limit above 10 MB will have valid uploads blocked client-side. The same regression is repeated for the 413 handler at line 246, which also now always reports 10 MB even for attachment uploads.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that hardcoding the client upload limit to 10 MB ignores configured per-type SiteSettings, causing divergence from server limits. Both also flag the same problem in the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle as WxH dimensions

`downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which passes `dimensions` to `gifsicle --resize-fit`. The new caller in UploadsController passes `"80%"`, but gifsicle expects a `WIDTHxHEIGHT` geometry, not a percentage, so animated GIFs that exceed the size limit will fail to be downsized (or error out) while the upload loop keeps retrying, and the oversized GIF is ultimately rejected or stored unshrunk.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" to the animated GIF resizing path results in gifsicle --resize-fit receiving a percentage instead of the required WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and proceeds with an oversized upload

The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value and never verifies the result after the loop. If `convert` fails (unsupported format such as SVG, corrupt image, missing tool) or 5 reductions of 20% are not enough, execution falls through to `Upload.create_for` with the still-oversized tempfile, producing an opaque validation failure instead of a meaningful error, after wasting up to 5 external-process invocations.

In-place ImageMagick conversion reads and writes the same file

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert <path>[0] ... <same path>`. ImageMagick is not guaranteed to handle in-place conversion safely: the output file can be truncated/created before the input is fully read, corrupting the upload (especially on failure mid-write, the original tempfile is destroyed). Convert to a separate temp file and atomically replace the original only on success.

Hardcoded 10 MB remote-download and unbounded direct-upload downsizing invite resource exhaustion

The API URL branch now always downloads up to 10 megabytes regardless of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`, and the new downsize block runs ImageMagick (up to 5 passes) on any image tempfile above the limit with no upper bound on its incoming size. A user can supply a very large/high-resolution image (within the web server's body limit) and force repeated decompression/conversion of it in the deferred job, consuming disproportionate CPU/memory; previously the download was capped at the configured image limit and oversized files were rejected cheaply by validation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser record

TopicUser.find_by can return nil (for example a logged-in user who opens or is forwarded an unsubscribe link for a topic they have never visited/interacted with, so no topic_users row exists). Lines 107-113 unconditionally call tu.notification_level and tu.save!, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. Use TopicUser.change (which creates the row) or guard/create the record before updating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil, and unconditional method calls on it cause a crash.

false_positives.candidate: State-changing unsubscribe is exposed as an unauthenticated-token GET request The unsubscribe action mutates notification_level on a plain GET, requires only the ambient login cookie (ensure_logged_in) and skips check_xhr. Any cross-site page can force a logged-in victim's browser to request /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe (e.g. via an tag) and downgrade/mute arbitrary topics for that victim without CSRF protection or a per-user/per-topic signed token. Email unsubscribe links should carry an unguessable token, or require a confirmation POST.

Unsubscribe action is not idempotent and progressively mutes the topic

If notification_level is above regular it is set to regular, otherwise it is set to muted. Re-opening the same email link, refreshing the landing page, or a mail scanner/prefetcher hitting the link a second time therefore takes a user who already unsubscribed (regular) and mutes the topic, which also removes it from topic lists — a stronger effect than requested. Repeated hits should converge on one terminal level (regular), not toggle downwards on each GET.

Unsubscribe template path does not match the topicUnsubscribe route

The Ember route is the top-level route 'topicUnsubscribe' (app-route-map.js.es6 line 13, routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6), whose template name resolves to 'topic-unsubscribe'. The template is instead placed at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which registers as 'topic/unsubscribe' (a nested topic route that does not exist). The unsubscribe page will therefore render with a missing/empty template and the notification dropdown in this file will not be shown.

Setting notification_level directly and calling save! bypasses TopicUser.change, which is the codebase path that stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, runs observe_after_save callbacks and publishes the /topic/:id MessageBus notification_level_change. Clients already viewing the topic and derived tracking state can therefore keep showing the old watching/tracking level after an unsubscribe until a reload, and the change is not recorded with a reason/time.

Global unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url for every email that uses it

unsubscribe_link is interpolated by Email::MessageBuilder for any mail built with add_unsubscribe_link: true (body and html_part), using template_args merged from the caller's opts. The new template unconditionally references %{unsubscribe_url}, but only UserNotifications#send_notification_email supplies unsubscribe_url; any other current/future caller with add_unsubscribe_link and no unsubscribe_url will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or render a broken link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be conditional or a default unsubscribe_url should be provided, and no new spec covers the unsubscribe controller action or an email built without unsubscribe_url.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed in-place edit uses macOS-only syntax and breaks on Linux

sed -i '' -E ... is BSD/macOS syntax; GNU sed on Linux interprets the empty string as a filename and errors out, so updating an existing GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in .env fails for Linux developers. Use a portable form (e.g. sed -i.bak and remove the backup, or detect the OS).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: using macOS/BSD sed syntax with an empty string after -i fails with GNU sed on Linux.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is always formatted in en-US locale

The timestamp is formatted with new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', ...) regardless of the user's configured locale obtained via useLocale. Non-English users will see US-style dates (e.g. MM/DD/YYYY) inconsistent with the rest of the localized UI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: date formatting hardcodes 'en-US' instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, resulting in incorrect or inconsistent localized date representations.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not invalidate the connected-calendars query

The deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls onSuccess, unlike disconnectMutation below it which invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations on settle. When onChanged/onSuccess is undefined (or does not refetch), the parent keeps the old query data, so cacheUpdatedAt remains set, the 'Cache Status / Delete cached data' entry stays visible, and the user sees stale status immediately after a successful deletion.

Cache status ignores cache expiry

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows for the credentials with no expiresAt filter, while getCachedAvailability only serves rows with expiresAt >= now. Credentials whose cache expired (one month after write) will therefore still report a cacheUpdatedAt in connectedCalendars, display 'Cache Status' in the UI, and offer to delete data that is never actually served.

Handler bypasses the calendar-cache disabled/mock repository path

The handler directly instantiates the concrete CalendarCacheRepository instead of going through the CalendarCache initialization that substitutes CalendarCacheRepositoryMock when calendar cache is disabled. Every connectedCalendars request now performs a CalendarCache groupBy query and can surface cache status even for users/organizations where the calendar-cache feature is disabled, adding an unconditional DB query to a hot settings endpoint.

updateManyByCredentialId accepts the wrong Prisma input type

The method types data as Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput but passes it to prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany, which expects SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput. UpdateInput permits nested relation operations (e.g. user: { connect }) that updateMany cannot execute, so the public repository signature promises operations that will fail or fail type-checking at the Prisma call; it should use the UpdateMany mutation input type.

dev:cron now depends on undeclared, unpinned tsx fetched via npx

The script was changed from ts-node (declared in devDependencies) to 'npx tsx', but tsx is not declared in this package's dependencies. On a fresh/offline install npx will try to download an unpinned package from the registry, making the script non-reproducible and failing without network access; tsx should be added as a pinned devDependency or the ts-node invocation kept.

New destructive deleteCache mutation has no tests

This PR adds a mutation that deletes all CalendarCache rows for a credential, guarded only by the credential-ownership check in this new handler, plus the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds repository method, with no tests covering: deleting one's own cache, rejecting another user's credentialId, and returning cache status per credential. A regression in the ownership where-clause would let one user purge another user's calendar cache without any test failing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects slots covered by any one of multiple ranges and ignores slot end

The code uses find() for any workingHour on that weekday where the slot start is before its startTime or after its endTime, and sets both start and end from the slot start (lines 141-142, so eventLength is never checked). With split availability on one day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) a 09:00 slot matches the second range as 'outside' and is rejected, while a slot starting inside a range but ending after it ends is accepted. This breaks fixed-host filtering for users with split or multiple same-day ranges.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that both start and end are calculated from the slot start, causing the slot's actual end to be ignored. This matches the golden issue, despite also describing a separate multiple-range filtering bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty (unavailable-day) override check compares Dayjs objects with ===

dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) compares two distinct Dayjs object references, so it is always false. An override with start == end, used to mark a whole day unavailable, is therefore never detected as such; slots at/after that instant fall through, have dateOverrideExist=true, and are returned as available instead of being blocked for the day.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: comparing separately constructed Dayjs objects with === checks reference identity rather than date values, causing the equality check to always fail. The candidate also explains the resulting unavailable-day override failure.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override slots bypass busy-time checks

When a slot's date matches a date override, checkIfIsAvailable sets dateOverrideExist and returns true at lines 133-135 before reaching the busy.every() check at line 153. Therefore a fixed (or round-robin) host who has a calendar/Cal booking overlapping a slot on an override day is reported available for that slot, so overlapping bookings can be created precisely on override days.

Override conversion assumes timeZone is present and loses day-boundary crossing

TimeRange.timeZone is optional (added as timeZone? in schedule.d.ts) and other getSlots callers need not supply it, yet lines 212-213 unconditionally call .tz(override.timeZone); with undefined this does not give the organizer offset. Additionally lines 218-223 reduce the shifted start/end to hour*60+minute, discarding the date: an override shifted by the invitee/organizer offset across midnight produces endTime <= startTime (or a time belonging to the adjacent invitee day), which buildSlots discards via start >= end, so those override slots disappear instead of appearing on the correct day.

No test for the round-robin fixed-host override fix

The PR description claims fixed hosts' date overrides are now honoured for round-robin events, but the only added test (lines 788-804) re-queries the existing single-user date-override scenario in Asia/Dhaka and asserts identical UTC slots. There is no scenario with schedulingType ROUND_ROBIN, a fixed host with an override and a non-fixed host, nor an unavailable/empty override or a busy time on an override day, so the new checkIfIsAvailable filtering path for fixed hosts is untested and regressions in it would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increment uses stale snapshot instead of atomic increment

Both increments write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read by the earlier findMany. If two cron invocations (or overlapping executions of the same invocation window) process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both read the same count and both write the same count+1, losing an increment; likewise a concurrent successful scheduling can be overwritten in effect because the failure writer does not condition on scheduled:false. This lets a permanently failing reminder be attempted more than the intended two times and makes the >1 deletion threshold unreliable. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` (ideally guarded by scheduled:false).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify lost retryCount increments caused by writing a stale reminder.retryCount + 1 under concurrency, including both update paths, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment. The candidate's additional scheduling concern does not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The deleteMany OR's second branch only checks retryCount > 1, without method: WorkflowMethods.SMS (and without scheduled: false). Because WorkflowReminder rows are shared by EMAIL, SMS and WHATSAPP methods, any non-SMS reminder whose retryCount ever exceeds 1 will be deleted by this SMS cron, losing its referenceId/cancellation handle even though this job never processed it. The SMS-only condition from the original first branch does not carry over to the second OR branch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch lacks a WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing the SMS reminder job to delete non-SMS reminders. The candidate's additional details do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing recipient or empty message never increments retryCount

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` when twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy, or in the catch block. If sendTo is null/empty (e.g. booking has no smsReminderNumber / step has no sendTo) or the rendered message is empty, neither branch runs: the reminder stays scheduled:false with retryCount 0 and is re-fetched and re-processed on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes. This is one of the permanent-failure modes the PR is meant to bound, so those reminders are still retried indefinitely.

Unhandled update in catch block can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits prisma.workflowReminder.update without any nested error handling. If that update rejects (e.g. the reminder was deleted by the top-of-run deleteMany of a concurrent invocation, a booking-cancellation cleanup, or a transient DB error - Prisma throws P2025 for a missing record), the exception propagates out of the per-reminder loop, the handler returns 500, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are never processed in this run. Previously the catch only logged and the loop continued.

Public findMany API is removed without migrating any callers

This change replaces the service's public findMany(findManyArgs) method with getBaseConditions() and only updates this service and its integration test. Any existing caller that invoked InsightsBookingService.findMany to fetch BookingTimeStatusDenormalized rows will now fail TypeScript compilation/runtime, and no caller in this PR is migrated to construct a $queryRaw query with the returned conditions. EventResult.externalId is therefore undefined, and referencesToCreate stores externalCalendarId undefined for that calendar event. Subsequent reschedule/cancel/update operations cannot address the specific external calendar the event was created on and may target primary/the wrong calendar.

Recurring cancellation deletes the first calendar reference for every credential and repeats per outer reference

Inside the new loop over all bookingCalendarReference entries, the recurring branch maps over all organizer calendar credentials and for each updated booking uses `updBooking.references.find(ref => ref.type.includes('_calendar'))`, i.e. always the first calendar reference regardless of the credential being iterated or the outer reference. With multiple hosts/references this issues duplicate deleteEvent calls with mismatched credential/uid/externalCalendarId pairs, potentially failing to delete some hosts' events and repeatedly deleting others.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach makes calendar/video cancellation fire-and-forget and bypasses try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` is never awaited: forEach ignores the returned promises, and the surrounding try/catch cannot catch rejections from the async callback. Reschedule() proceeds to send the reschedule email and return true before (and regardless of whether) the old calendar/video events are deleted, so failures are silently lost as unhandled rejections and stale events can remain. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: async callbacks passed to forEach produce unawaited promises, allowing cleanup to run fire-and-forget and bypass surrounding try/catch error handling. Its proposed fix, awaiting Promise.all with map, also matches the golden recommendation.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are eagerly started, not lazy

Every value is an already-executed import() call in the object literal, so importing appStore immediately initiates loading all ~30 app modules instead of loading only the requested app on first use. This defeats the stated purpose of the PR and keeps the startup/bundle-evaluation cost (and side effects) of every app for any caller that needs just one. The promises should be wrapped in thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with callers invoking them. A related consequence is that a failing optional app creates a rejected promise at import time that may surface as an unhandled rejection even if that app is never used.

requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` discards the promises returned by the async callback. The mutation immediately sends the reschedule email and webhooks and returns, so the previous calendar/video events may still exist (or fail silently as unhandled rejections) when the user reschedules via the emailed link. Await the deletions, e.g. with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`, before proceeding.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The encoded prefix is 2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type, so the grant shortcut is substring(4,6), not substring(3,5). The matcher also returns false when substring equals expectedGrantShortcut and otherwise does not reject a mismatching grant at all. Consequently expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken will fail for correct tokens and pass for wrong grant types, masking regressions. It should be: if (!items[0].substring(4,6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false; (with a length guard to avoid StringIndexOutOfBounds).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same two problems as the golden comment. The substring should be (4,6) instead of (3,5), and the equality check is inverted so that a matching grant returns false.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks all custom grant-type factories

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an SPI implemented by out-of-tree/custom grant types. Adding getShortcut() as an abstract interface method means every existing custom factory no longer compiles and, if deployed as an old binary, throws AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates provider factories. This is a breaking SPI change for a feature that could degrade gracefully. The method should be a default method (e.g. returning the unknown shortcut) so existing grants continue to work.

Copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context removed and constructor can now NPE

The public Context(Context) copy constructor is deleted, breaking any grant implementation that cloned/modified the context before processing. In addition the remaining constructor now unconditionally calls formParams.getFirst(GRANT_TYPE), so code that constructed a Context with null formParams (previously valid) now throws NullPointerException at construction. Both changes break external grant types without a deprecation path.

Token issuance now fails for unknown or unregistered grant types

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() copies the raw GRANT_TYPE attribute into AccessTokenContext, and encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException if that string has no registered shortcut. TokenManager.initToken() now calls this for every access token, so any flow or custom grant that sets a grant_type value that is not exactly a registered OAuth2GrantType factory id (or a custom provider returning a null/duplicate shortcut, which also causes a ConcurrentHashMap NPE in the factory refresh path) will fail token creation with a 500 instead of issuing a token. Previously such tokens were issued with a plain UUID. Encoding should fall back to the 'na' unknown shortcut rather than aborting issuance.

Lightweight-token detection uses ambient context client and can NPE or misclassify

getShouldUseLightweightToken(session) reads session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(...) (AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper line 86) and does not use the client from clientSessionContext. TokenManager.initToken() is invoked from flows where the KeycloakContext client is not set or differs from the client session's client (e.g. internally created/exchanged tokens), so this can throw NullPointerException during initToken or encode 'lt'/'rt' based on the wrong client. The client should be taken from clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient() and null-checked.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw recovery codes are handed to and persisted by user storage in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the generatedCodes list (the raw, human-usable recovery codes) as JSON and passes it as the UserCredentialModel challenge response to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Unlike the local path, which stores RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel data containing hashes of the codes, a user-storage provider that persists this input verbatim (as the PR's own BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at updateCredential/getCredentials) ends up storing all unused recovery codes in plaintext at rest. Anyone with read access to the external store then obtains valid second-factor bypass codes for the user. The codes should be hashed before leaving Keycloak, or the storage contract must require and document hashing, so federated persistence is not weaker than local persistence.

Federated recovery codes are never consumed or removed after successful use

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, the code only checks recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the model returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() and calls removeStoredCredentialById() when exhausted. For a federated credential this does not work: consumption/marking-used is performed by the local RecoveryAuthnCodes credential provider when it updates its stored credential, whereas a user-storage validator (such as the PR's BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(), which only compares the input against the stored list) does not mutate the stored codes, so allCodesUsed() stays false and the same code remains replayable indefinitely. Additionally removeStoredCredentialById() removes local DB credentials by id and cannot delete a credential held in user storage (federated credentials must be disabled/updated via the storage provider), so even an exhausted federated credential is not removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES regeneration path can be bypassed. Single-use semantics for recovery codes are therefore broken for federated users.

getCredential prefers federated over local without aligning with validation, risking wrong code state when both exist

getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if any exists and only falls back to the locally stored credential otherwise. This helper now drives both the login form's next-code number (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) and the post-login allCodesUsed()/removal decision (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), but credential validation through credentialManager().isValid() can be satisfied by the local credential provider. For a user who has both a stale local credential and a federated one (e.g. codes created locally before the storage started supporting the type, and then re-created in storage via the new fallback logic in CredentialHelper), the UI will prompt for the code number from the federated set and exhaustion will be evaluated against the federated set, while validation/consumption may act on the local set. The result is a wrong requested code index and failure to regenerate/remove the credential that was actually consumed. Lookup precedence must match the validator's precedence, or dual credentials must be prevented/deduplicated.

getCredentials dereferences MyUser without the null check used by sibling methods

The new getCredentials() does var myUser = getMyUser(user); and immediately accesses myUser.recoveryCodes (line 235) and myUser.otp (line 247). getMyUser() returns users.get(...), which is null for a username not present in the map, and sibling methods such as isConfiguredFor() and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() explicitly guard against that. If credential listing is invoked for a user not in this storage's map, the provider throws NullPointerException instead of returning an empty credential stream, breaking credential listing/account flows for such users.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled gating is only tested for metadata and its exit code is not asserted

The new test covers only `update-compatibility metadata` without `--features=rolling-updates` and only asserts the error message. It does not cover the separately added gating in `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` and does not assert exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`) for either subcommand. A regression that leaves `check` ungated, or returns the picocli software/usage error codes instead of 4, would therefore pass while breaking scripts and the operator flow that rely on distinguishing feature-disabled from recreate (3) and rolling (0).

Caution overstates that the operator will fail without rolling-updates

The new caution says that while in preview the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled, otherwise the Keycloak Operator will fail. That is not scoped to using `spec.update.strategy`, and it contradicts the PR's own operator test setup in UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment, where the default/null-strategy deployment returns before enabling `rolling-updates` and is still expected to deploy and upgrade. As written, users with ordinary CRs will believe every deployment must enable a preview feature or the operator fails; the text should be limited to deployments that use the update-strategy feature.

Exit code 4 is described as a compatibility verdict although no check ran

The table describes exit code 4 as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible' when the feature is disabled. In that case UpdateCompatibilityCheck and UpdateCompatibilityMetadata return before validating/reading metadata or computing compatibility, so compatibility is unknown rather than disproven. Scripts following this wording may permanently choose a recreate/downtime path for a merely misconfigured invocation instead of treating 4 as an enablement/configuration error distinct from the recreate verdict (3).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing all-clients resource causes NullPointerException during evaluation

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no instance resource exists the code loads the all-clients resource via getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls findByResource(server, resource) and later builds a ResourcePermission from it without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the 'Clients' resource is absent (for example in realms whose admin-permissions client was initialized before the Clients type existed, since init() returns early when the client already exists and never adds the new scopes/resources). true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: getResourceTypeResource can return null in hasPermission, and passing that null to findByResource causes a NullPointerException.

false_positives.candidate:
Role-mapping checks lose manage/admin fallback

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only evaluate the corresponding fine-grained scope for the client. They do not fall back to canManage(client), unlike the V1 evaluator where an administrator who can manage a client (including via the manage-clients admin role) can map its roles. A full realm admin or a user granted only the Clients 'manage' scope is therefore incorrectly forbidden from role/composite/client-scope role mapping in V2.

Resource display name is not resolved for Clients resources

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the type resource and resolves instance resources to usernames. Clients resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), but instance resources created by getOrCreateResource are named by client id and have no display name set, and the 'Clients' type resource is not translated to 'All clients'. Permission/resource representations for Clients will consequently expose a null/blank name instead of the client id or 'All clients'.

Removal listener can dispatch to V2 evaluator that throws on cleanup

The listener now runs whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but management() dispatches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is also enabled. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so when both features are enabled, role/client/group removal events invoke V2 cleanup and fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of disabling permissions. The guard needs to exclude the V2 case (or the dispatch needs to use the V1 evaluator for this cleanup).

The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

canManage() grants manage to holders of only the view scope

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the 'view' scope on all Groups passes canManage(). requireManage() is based on this method and is used e.g. by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup to create top-level groups, so a view-only FGAP admin can create groups (and perform other operations gated only by requireManage()). canManage() should require only the MANAGE scope, as canManage(GroupModel) on line 79 already does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs/names

Resources for Groups are looked up by name, where the resource name is the group ID (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and hasPermission(String) does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)). It then adds groupResource.getId() to the result, but callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser/getUsersCount and BruteForceUsersResource expect actual group IDs for the UserModel.GROUPS filter. In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, the resource's own ID is passed to hasPermission, which looks resources up by name, and that same ID is added to the result instead of the group ID (the resource name). Both note that evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource and that the user filters and counts end up wrong.

getResourceName has no handling for the new Groups resource type

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users resource type, returning the username for a user resource and 'All users' for the type resource. For the newly added Groups type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), but group resources created by getOrCreateResource have the group ID as their name and no display name set, so permission listings for group resources will show a null/blank or raw ID instead of the group name (and no 'All groups' label). Add the analogous Groups branch resolving the group by resource name and returning its name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle

The method contract in CryptoProvider is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) security provider, and callers use it for BC-specific algorithms and provider names. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a stock JDK is typically the SUN provider, not BouncyCastle. Any authz-client code path (or synced keycloak-client code path) that consults getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC capabilities will get the wrong provider and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider or behave differently. It should return null like WildFlyElytronProvider if no BC provider is available, or an actually-registered BC provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle, so the candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside this repository (custom server providers, downstream Elytron/FIPS variants, test doubles) will fail to compile and, if compiled against the old interface, throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts providers by order(). This should be a default method (e.g. returning a defined default priority) so existing providers keep working and only providers needing precedence override it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations. This is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now silently chosen non-deterministically instead of failing fast

Previously detectProvider() threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. Now it sorts by order() descending and silently ignores the rest, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200. If two of those are co-present (e.g. default + Elytron in WildFly, or default + FIPS), the winner depends only on unspecified ServiceLoader iteration order among equal keys, so a non-FIPS provider could be selected in FIPS mode or vice versa with only a debug log. Equal top orders should either retain the fail-fast error or have a deterministic, documented tie-break.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and only assert round-trip equality

The shared constructor creates one KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() key, which defaults to a 256-bit curve, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. asn1derToConcatenatedRS merely zero-pads/truncates r and s to algorithm.getSignatureLength()/2, so the round-trip assertion passes for ES384/ES512 even though no P-384/P-521 key or real signature of that size is ever produced or verified. The test never verifies the produced DER signature with Signature.verify(), so conversion defects for larger curves or leading-zero r/s values would go undetected. Each algorithm should generate a key on its matching curve and verify the converted signature cryptographically.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, making the concurrency assertion racy and leaking the thread

The test starts a reader thread at line 139 that loops while deletedAll is false, sets deletedAll to true at line 155, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty at line 157 without joining the thread. A request already in flight can still fail and add to caughtExceptions after the assertion, so a real concurrent-access failure can be missed and the test can pass spuriously. Conversely the unjoined busy-loop thread can outlive the test, continue issuing admin requests against a realm/client being torn down or reused, and pollute subsequent tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. The reader thread is never joined, and setting deletedAll then asserting right away creates a race in which exceptions added afterward are missed. That makes the test flaky.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the other lazy-delegate methods

The fix null-checks only getSubGroupsCount() at line 275, but getSubGroupsStream(String,Integer,Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer,Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String,Boolean,Integer,Integer) at line 268 still dereference modelSupplier.get() without a null check. If the group is deleted concurrently, the delegate lookup returns null exactly as in getSubGroupsCount(), so these methods throw NullPointerException instead of handling the deleted group. The reported concurrent-access NPE therefore remains reachable through subgroup listing/search, not just subgroup counting.

Unthrottled reader loop can overwhelm the test server and collect unbounded failures

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard therefore evaluates to False for every real flusher process. When _ensure_processes_alive detects a hang (is_alive() is True but healthy_since is stale), it skips process.kill() and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards. The hung process keeps running alongside its replacement, so two processes can concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produce for the same Redis shards, risking duplicate or racing segment flushes, while the hung process continues consuming resources. The guard should check against the spawn context's process type / BaseProcess, or duck-type on kill/terminate.

Because the flushers are SpawnProcess objects from the spawn context, this check is always False in production, so any flusher that does not exit promptly after stopped is set is never terminated. join() waits until the deadline for each process in sequence and then silently returns with daemon processes still alive, leaking processes and potentially leaving flushers running against Redis/Kafka after the consumer strategy has shut down. Use the mp_context process base type or hasattr-based termination instead.

Negative or zero flusher-process configuration crashes or disables flushing

The CLI option --flusher-processes accepts any int with no validation. A negative value flows through factory.py into SpanFlusher, where max_processes stays negative (only 0/None fall back via `or`), num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and the shard assignment loop then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failures when computing i % num_processes or indexing the map. Given the PR's core change is parallel flushing and supervision, a test should push spans through a multi-process (at least multi-thread via produce_to_pipe) flusher and assert each segment is produced exactly once, and/or simulate a dead/hung process and assert it is replaced.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore advance past a message that was never successfully processed, contradicting the strategy's documented 'only commits after successful processing' guarantee and causing permanent data loss on transient processing failures instead of redelivery.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can grow without limit

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns immediately after put(). Despite the docstring claiming natural backpressure, the Arroyo consumer will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing messages as fast as it can fetch them even if workers are stuck or slow, leading to unbounded in-memory growth/OOM and a huge backlog of fetched-but-uncommitted offsets.

Strategy close/terminate discards queued work by shutting down the shared pool

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit shutdown event and immediately calls queue_pool.shutdown() without first waiting for queues to drain (wait_until_empty is never used). FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True, so a worker exits at the top of its loop after its current item even if its queue still holds items. On Arroyo partition revocation/rebalance this abandons in-flight messages, and because the same pool is shared (see result_consumer factory), closing one strategy instance also kills the pool for any subsequently created strategy: queue.put then raises queue.ShutDown, which submit()'s catch-all converts into add+complete offset, silently committing unprocessed messages.

Catch-all in submit marks offsets complete for messages never enqueued

submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except and, on any exception, adds and immediately completes the offset. This conflates poison messages with transient failures: e.g. grouping_fn raising, queue shutdown raising queue.ShutDown, or the real decode_payload asserting on FilteredPayload (decode_payload asserts payload is not FilteredPayload) all cause the offset to become committable even though nothing was processed, silently dropping the message with only a log line.

Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread

_commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls commit_function (the Arroyo Commit callable supplied to create_with_partitions) from there. Arroyo processing strategies are driven single-threaded by StreamProcessor and the commit callable/consumer commit path is not documented as thread-safe; invoking it concurrently with the main consumer loop risks races with the processor's own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit logic and with partition assignment changes, potentially committing offsets for partitions no longer owned.

Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(group_key) % num_queues. For str keys hash() is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the 'consistent hashing' claimed in the docstring is not stable across restarts or across consumer processes: the same subscription is assigned to a different queue whenever the process restarts, breaking the ordering/affinity guarantee the pool exists to provide relative to any other process or previous incarnation. A stable digest (e.g. md5/sha like other Sentry grouping code) is required.

Committable-offset scan is O(offset range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) and is invoked every second by the commit loop. When one slow item blocks a partition (the exact scenario this PR targets), the outstanding window grows with throughput, so each scan walks an ever-larger range of integers doing two set lookups per offset, and all_offsets keeps every uncommitted offset in memory. A single stuck subscription can thus make commit processing progressively more expensive and delay commits for all partitions.

Queue pool and offset tracker are never reset on partition reassignment

The FixedQueuePool (and its OffsetTracker) is created once in the factory __init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. OffsetTracker state (all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed) is keyed only by Partition and is never cleared when partitions are revoked or reassigned, and last_committed starts at -1 regardless of the committed position Arroyo passes in the partitions mapping. After a rebalance, stale outstanding entries from the previous assignment can permanently block commits for a reassigned partition, or stale last_committed state can cause incorrect committable calculations for a partition this consumer no longer owns or newly owns at a different position.
