Cursor values are client-supplied (`Cursor.from_string` accepts a negative offset), and with `enable_advanced_features=True` the code passes `cursor.offset` straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, claiming in comments that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this is safe. Django querysets explicitly raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so a crafted `cursor=...:-5:...` request crashes the endpoint (500/DoS); if the queryset were ever a plain sequence the same code would instead wrap around and return rows from the end of the result set, bypassing the intended page window. The same unguarded negative-offset path was left in `BasePaginator.get_result` (line 182) for `is_prev` cursors, affecting all existing paginators.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly states that BasePaginator.get_result leaves an unguarded negative-offset path for is_prev cursors, so negative offsets reach queryset slicing. This is the same issue as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime ordering it is wired into

`get_item_key` does `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute, copying `Paginator` instead of `DateTimePaginator`. `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError` on the first result whenever `optimized_pagination=true` is used by a superuser/global-access member. The optimized audit-log path therefore 500s rather than paginating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime value because order_by is '-datetime', which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Insert-time eviction silently discards spans and can produce incomplete segments

When a segment exceeds 1000 members, `zpopmin` silently removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans without any metric, log, or marker that the segment was truncated. The remaining segment is later flushed as if complete. This replaces the previous `_load_segment_data` behaviour of detecting oversized segments and logging/metric-ing `segment_span_count_exceeded`, and changes the cap from `max_segment_spans=1001` in Python to a hardcoded 1000 in Lua, so legitimate large segments lose spans invisibly.

Redirect chain traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop that follows `span-buf:sr:` redirects now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper segment trees may not be joined correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 will now be split into multiple segments (wrong `set_key`, wrong segment/root attribution) where they previously assembled correctly, with no test covering deep chains near the new limit.

SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks on existing Redis data during deployment

`process_spans` now `zadd`s to `span-buf:s:*` keys and the Lua script uses `zcard`/`zunionstore`, while `_load_segment_data` uses `zscan`. Any segment keys already stored as plain SETs by the previous version (written with `sadd`) will raise Redis WRONGTYPE errors when touched by the new code, so in-flight segments at deploy time will error out / be lost instead of being flushed. No migration, dual-read, or versioned key prefix is provided.

Flush-side max_segment_spans guard removed with no replacement for pre-existing/oversized keys

The check that skipped and logged segments with more than `max_segment_spans` spans was deleted from `_load_segment_data`. The only remaining cap is the new Lua insert-time cap of 1000, which does not apply to keys created before this change, keys written by still-running old consumers during a rolling deploy, or the `max_segment_bytes`-only path; such segments are now loaded and flushed regardless of span count, and `self.max_segment_spans` is left as dead configuration.

Required end_timestamp_precise lookup can crash the consumer on spans lacking the field

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message without that field (the existing consumer test payload did not include it until this PR added it). A single such message fails `process_batch` and, being redelivered, can poison-pill the batch instead of being handled or defaulted. The new `Span.end_timestamp_precise` field in buffer.py is likewise a required positional field, breaking any other `Span(...)` constructors that were not updated.

Unrelated, undocumented optimized_pagination switch changes audit-log API behaviour

This PR is described as a spans-buffer optimization, but it adds a new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter and a superuser/`has_global_access` gate that swaps the audit-log endpoint to a different paginator class. That is an unreviewed API contract/behaviour change bundled into the spans change: cursor format and results now depend on the caller's privileges, and (per the paginator defects) the privileged path is broken, with no endpoint tests covering either branch.

No test exercises eviction, the 1000-span cap, or deep redirect chains

The test changes only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing Span constructions (all with the identical timestamp 1700000000.0). Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify which spans `zpopmin` evicts (including whether the root/segment span can be evicted, invalidating `has_root_span` flushing), nothing verifies ordering by differing `end_timestamp_precise` scores after `zunionstore` merges, and nothing covers redirect chains over 1000 hops. The core new behaviour of the PR is therefore untested, as is the new OptimizedCursorPaginator/audit-log path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key relies on Python hash() and the invalidation helper is never wired up

Eligibility is cached under a key built from hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) and invalidate_upsampling_cache recomputes the same expression, but no code path calls invalidate_upsampling_cache when the project allowlist option changes. Combined with hash-collision risk between different project sets, one project set can briefly serve another set's cached eligibility and, more importantly, allowlist removals keep upsampling (and additions keep not upsampling) until TTL expiry with no invalidation hook despite the helper suggesting otherwise. Use a deterministic, collision-resistant key (e.g. the joined project ids) and either call invalidation on option change or remove the dead helper.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the cache key built with Python's hash() and recommend a deterministic key. The candidate's reasons differ: it cites collision risk and missing invalidation calls, not hash randomization across processes. Still, it points to the same code issue and the same fix, so it is a partial-to-good match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset (which the dashboard-widget split logic can change to discover or keep as the metrics dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead of scoped_dataset. When a metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced request is split into a Discover error query, upsampling is wrongly skipped; conversely a transaction-like split can be transformed based on the original dataset even though the executed dataset/query is not error data. The transform decision must be made for the dataset actually executed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset`. As a result, upsampling is skipped when the dashboard split sends a metrics request to discover. The candidate states this identical consequence.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count is only registered on Discover but is generated for the errors dataset

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count() whenever _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True, and that helper returns True unconditionally for the errors dataset. However the new SnQLFunction is only added to the Discover dataset's function_converter; the errors dataset has its own function converter without upsampled_count. Any events-stats request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore fail query validation/building (unknown function) instead of returning upsampled counts.

Substring check treats negated error filters as error-focused queries

_is_error_focused_query does a raw substring search for 'event.type:error', so queries such as '!event.type:error', '-event.type:error', or 'event.type:transaction OR !event.type:error' are classified as error-focused. The endpoint will then rewrite count() to sum(sample_weight) over predominantly transaction/non-error rows, where sample_weight is not meaningful/populated, returning zero or badly undercounted series instead of the real count.

sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no fallback for rows whose sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects will normally contain historical events and events ingested without client sampling information; ClickHouse sum() ignores NULLs (and yields NULL/0 for an all-NULL bucket), so those events silently disappear from upsampled counts rather than counting as 1 each. A safe aggregate needs a per-row default such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

Accidental gitlink/subproject file committed

This adds a file `sentry-repo` containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a', i.e. an accidental nested-repository gitlink. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, will confuse tooling/checkouts, and should be removed before merge.

Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query inspects request.GET['query'], but _get_event_stats executes the `query` argument passed through get_event_stats_data and the dashboard split logic, which can differ from the raw GET parameter (split code appends 'AND !event.type:transaction', callers can supply modified queries). Eligibility can therefore be decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, causing missed upsampling for split error queries or transforms applied to non-error executions. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility check instead of re-reading the request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the permission-cache key prefix

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping/length-prefixing, so distinct tuples such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key; Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource. The key also uses the same 'perm_<uid>_<action>' prefix as userPermCacheKey in the same underlying cache, so crafted/extended components can collide with a permission entry (bool vs map JSON), causing spurious cache misses/corrupt entries.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same problem. userPermDenialCacheKey joins its components with '_' and no escaping, so components that contain underscores produce colliding keys and incorrect denial cache hits. The extra point about the shared prefix with userPermCacheKey does not change that the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache prevents newly granted/created resources from becoming accessible until TTL expiry

Check returns Allowed:false solely from permDenialCache before consulting fresh DB permissions, and no path clears a denial entry when permissions change or when getIdentityPermissions later refreshes permCache for another request. A user checked before creating/being granted a dashboard or folder (or before a grant propagates) is therefore still denied for the full shortCacheTTL (30s), partially defeating this PR's goal of letting creators immediately fetch newly created resources. Only TTL expiry unblocks them.

Denial is cached even when the denial may be caused by a stale folder tree

On the DB-recheck path, checkPermission -> checkInheritedPermissions still uses buildFolderTree's folderCache (30s TTL); permissions are refreshed but the folder hierarchy is not. A dashboard in a newly created/moved folder can thus be denied because ancestors are missing from the stale tree, and line 154 then promotes that possibly-stale result into permDenialCache for another TTL, extending the incorrect denial beyond the folder-cache expiry and making it immune to the permission refresh.

List still returns stale cached permissions with no revalidation

List accepts getCachedIdentityPermissions as authoritative whenever present and never re-queries the DB, unlike Check which falls back when the cached set does not contain the requested resource. A newly created dashboard/folder (or newly granted scope) will therefore be omitted from List results until permCache expires, so the PR's stated fix for fetching newly created dashboards/folders does not work for list/fetch-many flows that rely on List.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled KeyError

integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes every pre-existing Integration row has a sender dict with a login. Integrations created before sender was recorded (or created without that metadata) have no such key, so re-adding such an installation to an organization after its OrganizationIntegration was removed raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the graceful github-integration-failed page or a completed install. The lookup should use .get() chaining and decide explicitly how to handle absent sender data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is accessed without checking that the sender key exists, which raises a KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not exist yet

When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch immediately calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state github_authenticated_user against the installer/sender. The sender is only available from the webhook-created Integration, so this path is taken whenever the GitHub installation webhook has not yet created the Integration (a normal race between the install redirect and webhook delivery, and the path used by the ordinary fresh-install flow in the tests). An attacker who installed the app can therefore complete linking from a different authenticated GitHub account simply by finishing the pipeline before the webhook creates the row, defeating the validation this PR adds.

Token exchange network errors are not converted to the installation error page

safe_urlopen() is called outside the try block, which only wraps safe_urlread()/decoding. If GitHub's access-token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or returns an HTTP error that safe_urlopen raises for, the exception propagates out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and produces a 500 rather than the 'Invalid installation request' failure page promised for bad/reused codes and token failures. get_user_info() on line 434 has the same unhandled-failure exposure for the subsequent /user call.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The rewritten test_installation_not_found supplies a deliberately wrong state (ddd023...) on the second request, so OAuthLoginView rejects it for state mismatch and asserts 'Invalid installation request.' The request never reaches GitHubInstallation/build_integration, so the stubbed 404 from GET /app/installations/{id} and the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' IntegrationError path are no longer exercised despite the test name; a regression in 404 handling would pass unnoticed.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering

The cached branch collects identity-provider IDs and then the matching models into a HashSet and returns identityProviders.stream(). HashSet iteration order is unspecified and unrelated to the JPA delegate's ordering, so callers of getForLogin that consume the stream in order (e.g. take the first matching broker) can now observe a different, unstable provider order compared with the uncached path. Preserve encounter order (e.g. LinkedHashSet / ordered list) when materialising the cached IDs.

Login-cache update check compares an organization-aware original against a raw updated model

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is called from update() with 'original' obtained via getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): its isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization is disabled. The 'updated' model is the raw caller-supplied model whose isEnabled() only reflects the IdP flag, while the JPA getForLogin query that built the cache also only checks the IdP enabled flag. For an IdP in a disabled organization that is enabled/public (so its ID is in the cached login list), an update that sets hideOnLogin/linkOnly therefore yields predicate(original)=false and predicate(updated)=false and skips invalidation, leaving the now-hidden/link-only IdP's ID in the cached login list; callers such as OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-check isEnabled, so it can still be offered on the login page. Compute the original predicate from the unwrapped stored model (or the same semantics as the JPA query) before deciding to skip invalidation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is dead, inverted logic that always returns false

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false in the if branch and false unconditionally afterwards, so the feature-flag check has no effect and the function name/contract is misleading. The current behavior (always disabled) matches the PR intent, but a future maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions behind the flag will find flipping the toggle does nothing and may 'fix' the wrong branch, accidentally re-enabling it insecurely. Make the disable explicit (e.g. return false with a comment referencing the CVE/removal, or delete the helper and inline the rejection) instead of leaving inverted dead logic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say enableSqlExpressions has flawed or inverted logic that always returns false, so SQL expressions are disabled no matter what the flag says. The candidate frames the always-disabled result as matching the PR's intent, but it points to the same code issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command construction bypasses the new disabled check

UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled; only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in reader.go has the new gate. This legacy entry point is therefore protected only indirectly because the stub DB makes sql.TablesList fail, returning a misleading BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' instead of an explicit disabled/not-implemented rejection. If the DuckDB-backed DB implementation is restored or replaced, this path will silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 surface without passing through the reader check. Gate both construction paths (or remove/stub UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand) so disabling does not depend on a downstream stub error.

No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected even with the feature flag on

This is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI via DuckDB SQL expressions), but the PR adds no test asserting that a QueryTypeSQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path cannot execute SQL. Without such a test, restoring the go-duck dependency or simplifying enableSqlExpressions back to a plain flag check would reintroduce the vulnerability with no failing test. Add tests covering both entry points with the flag on and off.

go.work.sum churn is inconsistent with the go.mod/go.sum dependency removal

go.mod/go.sum drop go-duck and its transitive deps (apache/thrift, klauspost/asmfmt, minio/asm2plan9s, minio/c2goasm, JohnCGriffin/overflow), yet go.work.sum re-adds hashes for several of those same modules while dropping unrelated ones (Azure azblob, google go-replayers). This suggests the workspace sums were not regenerated with go work sync after the removal and may fail verification or resurrect the removed DuckDB transitive graph for other workspace modules. Regenerate and verify go.work.sum so the vulnerable dependency is actually gone from the whole workspace, not just the main module.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check under write lock causes duplicate loads and cache replacement

After acquiring the exclusive Lock at line 48, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. Two concurrent cold-cache callers in non-Dev mode can both pass the RLock check with ret==nil, then sequentially each perform readWebAssetsFromFile (and SetContentDeliveryURL) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache, with the first caller returning a pointer that is no longer the cached one. This wastes I/O and can yield different EntryPointAssets instances to concurrent callers; re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after Lock and returning it would make the fast path race-free and single-load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired in the double-checked locking pattern in GetWebAssets.

false_positives.candidate:
Mutex only guards the pointer, shared mutable EntryPointAssets is still returned to all callers

GetWebAssets returns the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer stored in the global cache to every caller. The new RWMutex protects only reading/writing the pointer variable, not the pointed-to struct/slices. Any caller that mutates the returned value (as this function itself does via result.SetContentDeliveryURL at line 64) races with concurrent readers of the cached object. The fix is incomplete unless callers are guaranteed never to mutate the result; returning a copy/clone on the cached path (or documenting/enforcing immutability) is needed to fully eliminate the shared-global-state race described in the PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log 'Annotations/Tags to clean' and 'cleaned ...' via r.log.Error on every batch, including successful batches where err is nil. This will emit error-level logs (often wired to alerting/error reporting) for normal operation and each message embeds the full ids slice, which can be tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes, creating huge noisy log lines. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same problem: routine or debug information is logged at Error level, which pollutes error logs, and both suggest using Debug or Info instead. The candidate also mentions the full ID lists being dumped, but its core concern is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval reduced 10x without justification

The global cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations) now runs 10x more often, not just annotation cleanup. This unrelated change increases DB and filesystem load on all Grafana instances and partially works against the goal of reducing MySQL contention from annotation cleanup. true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and its effect of raising DB load and contention. The candidate makes the same point and adds more detail.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

For SQLite with a large batch size, deleteByIDs builds the IN (...) list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop over all ids. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a 32767-ID list (as exercised by the new test) is O(n^2) in bytes copied and can take seconds and large allocations before the DELETE runs. Use strings.Builder (already imported) to build the list linearly.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

It also flags a mix-up in DeleteCollection itself, which is the method the golden comment names. However, its DeleteCollection point describes the opposite direction (the legacy call using recordStorageDuration), and its storage-failure points are about Create and Update. In DeleteCollection the async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency is counted as storage latency. Delete success at line 106 also passes `name` in place of the kind used by every other call, creating inconsistent/high-cardinality metric labels. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says Delete success passes `name` instead of the kind used by every other call, which makes metric labels inconsistent. That is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate also raises other problems, but it does cover this one.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled

Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) derive the legacy timeout context from ctx, which is the incoming request context embedded with the logger. The Kubernetes API handler cancels that context when the request returns, and Mode 3 returns immediately after spawning the goroutine. The legacy operation therefore races request completion and will often receive context.Canceled before writing, silently defeating the stated safety copy to legacy storage. The goroutine should derive from a detached context (for example context.WithoutCancel or a background context, preserving needed values) before applying the 10-second timeout.

Async Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object already written to unified storage

Storage.Update has already consumed objInfo to compute the updated object from the unified-storage version. The goroutine then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update, which will fetch the legacy (different) old object and call UpdatedObject again. That second computation can carry the unified-storage ResourceVersion/UID state and fail optimistic-concurrency or validation against legacy, or produce different content than what was committed to unified storage. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in updateWrapper carrying the exact object returned by Storage.Update; dropping that wrapper is a regression for the dual-write update path.

Async Create passes the storage-mutated input object to legacy Create

d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...) is commonly implemented by mutating the passed-in obj in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, creation timestamp, generated name). The goroutine then passes that same obj to d.Legacy.Create. Legacy create can therefore see a non-empty ResourceVersion/UID and reject the create, or create a legacy record whose identity/RV does not match a fresh create. Legacy should receive a copy cleared/derived from the returned created object (as other dual-writer modes do by stripping ResourceVersion), and doing the copy after Storage.Create also needs to happen before the caller can mutate the returned object.

Legacy async failures are never logged and a legacy panic crashes the process

All four async legacy goroutines only record a duration metric: the returned error is never logged (and in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection there is not even a log line naming the object on failure), and there is no recover. Because mode 3 promises legacy is written 'just as a safe measure', an operator cannot discover from logs that the safety copy is failing, and a panic in Legacy storage code inside the detached goroutine is not recovered by the HTTP handler middleware and will crash the server process.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes and share one mock for both stores

The tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock around the same *mock.Mock, so a call to either store satisfies indistinguishable expectations, and they never call AssertExpectations / AssertCalled for the legacy Create, Update or Delete paths (Delete/DeleteCollection tests do not even register legacy expectations). false_positives.candidate:

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every fallback computation. Before the database/settings are ready (boot, rake tasks, migrations, asset precompilation, or a nil/blank default_locale) SiteSetting can raise or return nil, and nil.to_sym raises NoMethodError. Because the I18n fallbacks backend invokes this on translation lookups, a routine translation can crash boot or request handling instead of falling back to :en.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, and missed fallbacks get cached

Fallback translations are loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale calling I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Background jobs, mailers, console/rake code and other non-controller paths set I18n.locale without this call, and I18n.translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only loads config.locale. In those contexts a key missing from the primary locale will be looked up in fallback locales whose YAML was never loaded, return a missing-translation string, and for argument-less translations that result is frozen into the LRU cache keyed only by key+locale+backend, poisoning later web requests until reload.

The LRU cache key is "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}" but the resolved value now depends on FallbackLocaleList, i.e. on SiteSetting.default_locale at lookup time. If an admin changes the site default locale, or a translation is first resolved before its fallback locale is loaded, the cached value for the user locale remains stale/frozen and is served indefinitely (up to cache eviction/reload) instead of the translation from the new fallback locale.

I18n.fallbacks is replaced with a Hash that does not implement the Fallbacks API

In environments where Rails still sets config.i18n.fallbacks, Rails can also overwrite this object with a real Fallbacks instance that has no ensure_loaded!, making ApplicationController#set_locale raise NoMethodError.

Every fallback lookup performs a SiteSetting lookup

FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale on each invocation, and the fallbacks backend invokes [] for translation lookups (including repeated/missing keys). This adds a settings/cache lookup to hot I18n paths that the translate accelerator is specifically trying to keep fast, instead of computing and memoizing the chain per locale and invalidating it when the site locale changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

Unescaped referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript

request.referer is inserted verbatim inside a single-quoted JS string passed to postMessage. The controller only checks the referer's host, so a referer such as http://<embeddable_host>/'-alert(1)-' contains a quote that breaks out of the string and executes arbitrary script in the embed page on the Discourse origin. The referer must be JS/HTML-escaped (and reduced to an origin) before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without escaping, which creates an XSS risk. The candidate adds a concrete exploit example, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import stores attacker-controlled RSS/Atom or scraped page contents as a Post with cook_method raw_html. Post#cook returns raw verbatim for that method, and the cooked HTML is rendered raw in topic and embed views. No sanitization is applied on this path (PollFeed passes feed content straight through), so a feed item or embedded page containing <script>/event-handler markup becomes stored XSS for every forum visitor who views the imported topic.

Unauthenticated requests can flood the retrieve_topic job queue

Every GET for an unknown embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job. The 60-second throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieve, which only runs when a job is executed, not before enqueueing. Anyone who can present the embeddable referer can therefore issue many requests for distinct or identical URLs faster than jobs drain and fill Sidekiq with jobs that each may fetch remote pages/feed content, instead of throttling/deduplicating at enqueue time.

This test expects TopicRetriever.new/retrieve to be called during EmbedController#best, but the controller instead calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). The mock expectations can never be satisfied by the implementation under test, so this example fails and provides no coverage of the actual enqueued job arguments (user_id and embed_url).

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with no validation

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url) on the supplied URL before TopicEmbed.import's scheme check runs, and performs no host allowlist, private-address, or redirect validation. Callers that pass externally influenced URLs (e.g. thread links from a Disqus export) can make the server issue requests to internal/metadata addresses (SSRF) and import the response. Host validation in TopicRetriever does not protect this entry point.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Any existing caller passing separate width and height (5 positional arguments including opts) will now raise ArgumentError, breaking thumbnail/downsize paths that use the old signature. The two signatures must be merged into one method that handles both forms.

The downsize method is defined twice, and the second definition, which takes a dimensions parameter, overrides the first, which takes max_width and max_height. As a result, existing callers that pass separate width and height arguments break.

Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle as WxH dimensions

`downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which passes `dimensions` to `gifsicle --resize-fit`. The new caller in UploadsController passes `"80%"`, but gifsicle expects a `WIDTHxHEIGHT` geometry, not a percentage, so animated GIFs that exceed the size limit will fail to be downsized (or error out) while the upload loop keeps retrying, and the oversized GIF is ultimately rejected or stored unshrunk.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: "80%" is passed to gifsicle --resize-fit on the animated path, but gifsicle expects WxH geometry, so animated GIFs fail to downsize.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and proceeds with an oversized upload

The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value and never verifies the result after the loop. If `convert` fails (unsupported format such as SVG, corrupt image, missing tool) or 5 reductions of 20% are not enough, execution falls through to `Upload.create_for` with the still-oversized tempfile, producing an opaque validation failure instead of a meaningful error, after wasting up to 5 external-process invocations.

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert <path>[0] ... <same path>`. ImageMagick is not guaranteed to handle in-place conversion safely: the output file can be truncated/created before the input is fully read, corrupting the upload (especially on failure mid-write, the original tempfile is destroyed). Convert to a separate temp file and atomically replace the original only on success.

The API URL branch now always downloads up to 10 megabytes regardless of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`, and the new downsize block runs ImageMagick (up to 5 passes) on any image tempfile above the limit with no upper bound on its incoming size. Lines 107-113 unconditionally call tu.notification_level and tu.save!, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. Use TopicUser.change (which creates the row) or guard/create the record before updating.

false_positives.candidate: State-changing unsubscribe is exposed as an unauthenticated-token GET request The unsubscribe action mutates notification_level on a plain GET, requires only the ambient login cookie (ensure_logged_in) and skips check_xhr. If notification_level is above regular it is set to regular, otherwise it is set to muted. Re-opening the same email link, refreshing the landing page, or a mail scanner/prefetcher hitting the link a second time therefore takes a user who already unsubscribed (regular) and mutes the topic, which also removes it from topic lists — a stronger effect than requested. Repeated hits should converge on one terminal level (regular), not toggle downwards on each GET.

The Ember route is the top-level route 'topicUnsubscribe' (app-route-map.js.es6 line 13, routes/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6, views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6), whose template name resolves to 'topic-unsubscribe'. The unsubscribe page will therefore render with a missing/empty template and the notification dropdown in this file will not be shown.

The new template unconditionally references %{unsubscribe_url}, but only UserNotifications#send_notification_email supplies unsubscribe_url; any other current/future caller with add_unsubscribe_link and no unsubscribe_url will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument (or render a broken link) when building the email. The per-topic sentence should be conditional or a default unsubscribe_url should be provided, and no new spec covers the unsubscribe controller action or an email built without unsubscribe_url.

This can resurrect/confuse dead bookings and sends misleading confirmed invites for events that will not happen. It should reject non-accepted and past bookings.

Calendar is updated with the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

credentials are loaded via getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and EventManager is built from the calling user, while evt.destinationCalendar belongs to the booking organizer. When the caller is a team admin or attendee (both explicitly authorized above), the organizer's calendar event is updated using the wrong user's credentials, so the calendar update will fail or target the wrong account even though the DB attendees were already added. Credentials/EventManager should be based on booking.user (already loaded with credentials in the query).

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison does not normalize letter case

Codes are generated as lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')) and the only normalization applied to user input is stripping '-'. A user who types or pastes their code in uppercase (a natural way to transcribe XXXXX-XXXXX codes) gets IncorrectBackupCode even though the code is correct. The same flaw exists in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61. Input should be lowercased (and trimmed) before comparison in both places.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue: backup code comparison is case-sensitive, so a correct code entered in uppercase fails validation. The candidate also explains why (codes are generated as lowercase hex) and recommends lowercasing the input before comparing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Single-use backup codes can be replayed concurrently

Consumption is a non-atomic read-check-update: two simultaneous logins with the same backup code can both read the stored array, both find the code at the same index, and both authenticate before either request writes back the array with that entry nulled. The documented 'exactly once' property of backup codes is therefore not enforced under concurrent requests; the code should be consumed with an atomic/conditional update or lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: concurrent logins can read, check, and update backup codes non-atomically, so one backup code can be accepted more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code can bypass password verification with a dummy TOTP field

Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, without exempting the new backup-code path. An attacker calling the credentials endpoint directly with a valid backup code, any non-empty totpCode value, and no/wrong password therefore skips verifyPassword, then enters the backupCode branch (which never validates the dummy totpCode) and is authenticated. A backup code, intended only as a second factor, becomes a single-factor passwordless login credential.

Backup codes are persisted and returned before TOTP setup is verified

Setup writes the encrypted backup codes (and TOTP secret) to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the setup response before the user has proven possession of the authenticator by completing the enable step. If setup is abandoned, valid backup codes for a not-yet-enabled account remain stored in the database, and the codes are already exposed to any client/script that called setup, even though the UI only displays them after enabling. Codes should be generated/confirmed at enable time, or at minimum not persisted until enable succeeds.

No test exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The new e2e coverage only downloads/copies the codes during setup; the file itself notes 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. The security-critical behaviors added in this PR — login with a backup code, rejection of a wrong code, single-use invalidation on reuse, missing-codes handling for pre-existing 2FA users, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — have no automated verification, so regressions or bypasses in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts would ship undetected.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

When externalCalendarId is falsy, `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` compares externalIds against undefined/null and therefore never matches, so selectedCalendar becomes undefined. Previously it fell back to the destination calendar's externalId. calendar.events.update is then called with calendarId undefined, so updates for bookings without an externalCalendarId on the reference fail instead of updating the destination calendar. true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Office365 createEvent always uses first host's destination calendar for every host

EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls createEvent once per destination calendar/credential, passing the matching credential, but Office365 (like Lark and CalDAV implementations) ignores the credentialId/externalId argument and uses only `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event with multiple hosts, the second host's credential is used to create an event on the first host's calendar ID, causing 404/authorization failures or a duplicate event on the wrong calendar rather than an event on the second host's calendar. The per-credential destination must be selected by credentialId.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment is about an interface signature mismatch: Lark and Office365 declare createEvent(event) without the credentialId parameter. The candidate says Office365 and Lark ignore the credentialId argument and always use destinationCalendar[0], which causes runtime errors with the wrong calendar. Both trace to the same implementations not taking or using credentialId, but the candidate frames it as a behavioral bug rather than an interface contract violation. This is a partial overlap.

false_positives.candidate:
Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty or null for Google Meet events

The code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. If destinationCalendar is null or an empty array (possible when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar, as handleNewBooking can set it to null), mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined and evaluating the Google Meet fallback throws a TypeError, breaking booking creation instead of falling back to Cal Video. It should use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

Google deleteEvent loses destination-calendar fallback and may delete from primary

When externalCalendarId is falsy, the find compares each destination calendar's externalId to that falsy value and returns undefined, so deleteEvent falls back to `primary`. Previously it used the stored destination calendar. Cancelling a booking whose event lives on a non-primary destination calendar will therefore target the wrong calendar (or 404/be silently resolved) and leave the actual event undeleted.

Lark createEvent always uses first host's destination calendar for every host

EventManager loops over all destination calendars and creates one event per credential, but Lark's createEvent still derives calendarId solely from `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. A collective booking's additional hosts therefore attempt creation on the organizer's Lark calendar with their own credentials, which fails or writes to the wrong calendar, so the multi-host fix does not work for Lark. It needs to pick the destination whose credentialId matches the credential used for this call.

Team destination calendars are silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null

evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizerUser has a destination calendar, and team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. With null, the optional-chain push is a no-op, so for a collective event where only non-organizer hosts have destination calendars, those calendars are lost and EventManager falls back to creating only one event on the first generic calendar credential. Initializing to [] or assigning the team array would preserve them.

Non-credential destinations create events without storing externalCalendarId/credentialId correctly

In the branch where a destination has no credentialId, createAllCalendarEvents calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing destination.externalId (unlike the credentialId branch at line 370). EventResult.externalId is therefore undefined, and referencesToCreate stores externalCalendarId undefined for that calendar event. Subsequent reschedule/cancel/update operations cannot address the specific external calendar the event was created on and may target primary/the wrong calendar.

Recurring cancellation deletes the first calendar reference for every credential and repeats per outer reference

Inside the new loop over all bookingCalendarReference entries, the recurring branch maps over all organizer calendar credentials and for each updated booking uses `updBooking.references.find(ref => ref.type.includes('_calendar'))`, i.e. always the first calendar reference regardless of the credential being iterated or the outer reference. With multiple hosts/references this issues duplicate deleteEvent calls with mismatched credential/uid/externalCalendarId pairs, potentially failing to delete some hosts' events and repeatedly deleting others.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach makes calendar/video cancellation fire-and-forget and bypasses try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` is never awaited: forEach ignores the returned promises, and the surrounding try/catch cannot catch rejections from the async callback. Reschedule() proceeds to send the reschedule email and return true before (and regardless of whether) the old calendar/video events are deleted, so failures are silently lost as unhandled rejections and stale events can remain. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. A forEach with an async callback leaves calendar/video deletions unawaited, so the try/catch is bypassed, rejections go unhandled and cleanup can be incomplete. Both suggest Promise.all with map as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are eagerly started, not lazy

Every value is an already-executed import() call in the object literal, so importing appStore immediately initiates loading all ~30 app modules instead of loading only the requested app on first use. This defeats the stated purpose of the PR and keeps the startup/bundle-evaluation cost (and side effects) of every app for any caller that needs just one. The promises should be wrapped in thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with callers invoking them. A related consequence is that a failing optional app creates a rejected promise at import time that may surface as an unhandled rejection even if that app is never used.

requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` discards the promises returned by the async callback. The mutation immediately sends the reschedule email and webhooks and returns, so the previous calendar/video events may still exist (or fail silently as unhandled rejections) when the user reschedules via the emailed link. Await the deletions, e.g. with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`, before proceeding.
